blocks.text: Management, Pharmacology & Complications

Epithelial cell connections include tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions. Tight junctions are responsible for creating a tight seal to prevent the paracellular movement of solutes or water through an epithelial or endothelial lining. Inflammation often impairs the efficacy of tight junctions.

Gap junctions facilitate electrical and chemical communication between neighboring cells via a connexon, a connecting cylinder with a central channel composed of connexin proteins (eg, connexin 43). In preparation for labor, increasing estrogen levels stimulate upregulation of connexin 43, increasing formation of gap junctions between individual myometrial cells. An increase in gap junction density allows the passage of small ions between neighboring myometrial cells, resulting in coordinated, synchronous labor contractions.

DD> Tight junctions (zonula occludens), composed of claudins and occludin, prevent paracellular passage of fluid and solutes. Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells help form the blood-brain barrier.

Cellular adhesion is the means by which one cell binds to another cell, surface, or matrix. The integrins are a family of transmembrane protein receptors that interact with the extracellular matrix by binding to specific proteins, including collagen, fibronectin, and laminin. Other adhesion molecule classes include the cadherins, selectins, and Ig superfamily members.
Embryology, Anatomy & Normal Physiology
Fibronectin is a component of the ECM. Renal mesangial cells grown in a medium that promotes the formation of the ECM would be expected to express increased levels of fibronectin mRNA.

Adhesion of cells to the extracellular matrix involves integrin-mediated binding to fibronectin, collagen, and laminin. Differential expression of integrin subtypes affects adhesion properties of individual cells, and has been found to correlate with malignant behavior in a number of tumors.

Fibronectin is essential for fibroblast migration and provides a pathway for migration during wound healing. Fibroblasts bind to peptide sequences within fibronectin, which guide them to the site of healing.

blocks.text: Photoaging — Etiology, Genetics

Photoaging is a product of excess exposure to ultraviolet A wavelengths and is characterized by epidermal atrophy with flattening of rete ridges. In addition, there is decreased collagen fibril production and increased degradation of collagen and elastin in the dermis.

blocks.text: Accessory nipples — Pathophysiology

Accessory nipples are the most common congenital breast anomaly resulting from failed regression of the mammary ridge in utero. They are usually asymptomatic but can become tender along with breast tissue during times of hormonal fluctuation.

topics.title: Acne
topics.summary: Acne vulgaris is an inflammatory disorder of pilosebaceous follicles. Contributing factors include hyperkeratinizat…

blocks.text: Pathophysiology & Mechanism

Acne vulgaris is an inflammatory disorder of pilosebaceous follicles. Contributing factors include hyperkeratinization and obstruction of follicles; sebaceous gland enlargement with increased secretion of sebum; colonization and proliferation in the gland by Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes; and follicular and perifollicular inflammation.
This patient's red papules and pustules on the face are consistent with inflammatory acne. The pathogenesis of acne involves the following:

Hyperkeratinization due to abnormal epithelial growth and differentiation of corneocytes leads to keratin plug formation in the pilosebaceous follicles. These blocked follicles are referred to as comedones (ie, whiteheads and blackheads).

In response to androgen stimulation (eg, during pubertal adrenarche), sebaceous glands enlarge (not involute) and increase production of sebum, a lipid-rich substance that facilitates obstruction of pilosebaceous follicles .

Cutibacterium acnes, an anaerobic bacteria that relies on sebum as a nutrient source, proliferates in occluded follicles, triggering an inflammatory response that results in the red papules and pustules characteristic of nodulocystic acne.
Management, Pharmacology & Complications

Risk factors for acne include increased androgen levels; obstruction of pilosebaceous glands by oil-based hair products; and mechanical irritation of skin follicles. Sports participation frequently triggers acne due to the use of tight-fitting clothing and protective gear.

Androgens stimulate follicular epidermal hyperproliferation and excessive sebum production, thereby promoting acne development. Androgenic steroid supplementation is a known cause of acne, especially in competitive athletes.

Tretinoin (a medication that decreases cohesion between epidermal cells and increases epidermal cell turnover) and other retinoids decrease comedone formation and are used as the first-line management of mild and moderate acne.

blocks.text: Atopic dermatitis & Clinical Correlation

rows: Mutation in epidermal barrier proteins (eg, filaggrin) leads to ↓ water content, ↑ permeability, ↑ inflammation Immune dysfunction (ie, Tspan-skewed response)
Acute: pruritic, erythematous patches & papules Infants: red extensor surfaces, trunk & face Children & adults: flexor surfaces Chronic: lichenified plaques

blocks.text: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a common, chronic inflammatory disorder caused by impairment of the skin's barrier function. Eczema presents with pruritus and erythematous papules and plaques and is associated with other atopic diseases, such as allergic rhinitis and asthma.

Atopic dermatitis increases the risk for allergic rhinitis, asthma, and food allergies, likely because of an immune response that favors IgE production. In addition, skin barrier dysfunction facilitates food allergen penetration and sensitization, increasing the risk for food allergies.

Key Tspan cytokines that trigger acute inflammation in atopic dermatitis are IL-4 and IL-13, and mechanisms include the following: Stimulation of plasma cell IgE production, which facilitates allergen sensitization and inflammation

IL-4 is produced by the TH2 subset of T helper cells. It facilitates proliferation of B cells and TH2 lymphocytes and stimulates antibody isotype switching to IgE which mediates type I hypersensitivity (allergic) reactions.
Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam
Atopic dermatitis is characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction (genetically mediated epidermal barrier dysfunction.), with chronic disease presenting as lichenification from repeated scratching.

This patient's atopic dermatitis has been successfully treated with a topical corticosteroid, leading to suppression of the typical inflammatory features (eg, pruritis, papules, vesicles, scales). However, chronic daily use of topical corticosteroids can cause cutaneous atrophy due to the inhibition of epidermal keratinocyte proliferation and fibroblast function. Local adverse effects of chronic topical corticosteroid therapy include cutaneous atrophy, telangiectasias, and corticosteroid-induced acne. Effects are more pronounced with high-potency corticosteroids and in areas of thin skin (eg, flexural areas).

blocks.text: Allergic contact dermatitis & Clinical Correlation

rows: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction Common triggers: poison ivy/oak, nickel, dyes, topical medications, skin care products
Acute: pruritic red, indurated plaques with vesicles/bullae Chronic: lichenification, fissuring
Clinical findings Patch testing for persistent cases
Avoidance of suspected allergen Topical or systemic corticosteroid

blocks.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. Initially, Langerhans cells travel to regional lymph nodes and present haptens to naive T cells, leading to clonal expansion. On reexposure to the hapten, sensitized T cells cause tissue destruction that manifests as pruritic erythema, vesicles, and/or bullae 2-3 days after exposure.
On reexposure, sensitized CD8+ T cells are recruited to skin and destroy tissue. Release of interferon gamma by T cells further amplifies the immune response.

Microscopically, acute ACD is characterized by spongiosis (ie, accumulation of fluid between keratinocytes in the epidermis). This patient developed pruritic, erythematous blisters and erosions on the thighs following application of a topical cream.
Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

Nickel is a common trigger and typically causes symptoms at the wrists (eg, watches), earlobes (eg, earrings), or umbilicus (eg, belt buckles). Corrosion of metal alloys by electrolytes in sweat releases soluble metal ions that trigger a hypersensitivity reaction. ACD is a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction occurring in 2 phases:

Allergic contact dermatitis (nickel allergy) is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction characterized by epidermal intercellular edema (ie, spongiosis) and an inflammatory infiltrate (eg, lymphocytes, eosinophils). Clinical findings can include vesicles, erythema, and pruritus for acute lesions and lichenification for chronic lesions.

topics.summary: Irritant contact diaper dermatitis is predominantly caused by skin barrier breakdown from exposure to urine and sto…

blocks.text: Irritant contact diaper dermatitis

Irritant contact diaper dermatitis is predominantly caused by skin barrier breakdown from exposure to urine and stool trapped within the diaper. Patients with frequent stooling (eg, diarrhea) are at increased risk because urease produced by fecal bacteria causes an increase in local skin pH, which allows for activation of proteolytic enzymes that disrupt the stratum corneum. Areas of macerated skin are then prone to frictional damage from the diaper, which further exacerbates the rash.

Dd> In contrast to candidal diaper dermatitis, another common diaper rash caused by a secondary yeast infection, irritant contact diaper dermatitis does not have skinfold involvement or satellite lesions (ie, discrete lesions beyond the borders of the main rash).

The treatment for irritant contact diaper dermatitis is a thick barrier ointment (eg, petrolatum) or paste (eg, zinc oxide), which provides the skin an adherent layer of protection from contact with the stool and urine. Other measures to reduce irritant exposure include frequent diaper changes and diaper-free periods.

topics.summary: Psoriasis is a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder that presents with scaly, erythematous plaques, typically …

blocks.text: Pathophysiology & Mechanism

Psoriasis is a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder that presents with scaly, erythematous plaques, typically on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees. In predisposed individuals, disruption of the epithelial barrier leads to activation of antigen-presenting dendritic cells and subsequently to a self-reinforcing inflammatory cascade characterized by recruitment and activation of T helper cells and proliferation of keratinocytes. Histopathologically, psoriasis is characterized by:
Hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum) and confluent parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum) produces the characteristic silvery scale on gross examination
Epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis) with elongated rete ridges correspond to the typical erythematous plaques
Neutrophilic foci in the stratum corneum and epidermis, which may coalesce to form microabscesses (Munro microabscesses)
Psoriasis is characterized by hyperkeratosis and confluent parakeratosis of the stratum corneum, and epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis) with elongated rete ridges.
Psoriasis — Pathophysiology

Psoriasis is histologically characterized by diffuse epidermal hyperplasia with elongated and clubbed rete ridges (corresponding to the typical erythematous plaques), confluent parakeratosis (producing the characteristic silvery scales seen on examination), and dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae (pinpoint bleeding).

First-line treatment options for localized psoriasis include topical corticosteroids (eg, diflorasone) and vitamin D analogs (eg, calcipotriene, calcitriol). Vitamin D analogs activate the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear transcription factor, resulting in inhibition of T-cell and keratinocyte proliferation and stimulation of keratinocyte differentiation. Corticosteroids also have anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties; their mechanism of action is complementary to vitamin D analogs, and the 2 agents work well in combination.

blocks.text: Ichthyosis vulgaris — Etiology, Genetics

Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by filaggrin gene mutations that result in defective keratinocyte desquamation. It is characterized by dry, scaly skin; manifestations are diffuse but are typically worse on the trunk and the extensor surfaces of the extremities.

blocks.text: Lichen planus — Pathophysiology

Lichen planus is an immune-mediated condition that presents with pruritic, pink papules and plaques, often with lacy, scaly, white markings (Wickham striae). The pathologic process in LP is characterized by a (CD8+) T cell–mediated response against cells along the dermal-epidermal junction. Although the etiology is unknown, the risk may be increased in patients with hepatitis C and those taking certain medications (eg, ACE inhibitors, thiazide diuretics). LP typically follows a chronic course with gradual, spontaneous remission within 2 years.

Histologic findings include hyperkeratosis (thickening of stratum corneum), lymphocytic infiltrates at the dermoepidermal junction, hypergranulosis (prominent granular layer), sawtooth rete ridges, and scattered eosinophilic colloid bodies.

topics.title: Pityriasis rosea
topics.summary: Pityriasis rosea is characterized by the acute onset of a pruritic patch followed by the development of numerous sm…

blocks.text: Pityriasis rosea — Clinical Presentation

Pityriasis rosea is characterized by the acute onset of a pruritic patch followed by the development of numerous smaller macules and patches in a recent viral illness. The individual patches of pityriasis rosea are oval in shape and scaly, and they have a scaly rim around the leading edge. This patient should be reassured that the condition will self-resolve in 6 to 8 weeks and can be treated symptomatically with topical corticosteroids in the meantime.

blocks.text: Pemphigus vulgaris — Clinical Presentation

Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune bullous disease characterized by autoantibodies directed against desmosomal proteins (eg, desmogleins). It presents with painful, flaccid bullae and erosions affecting the skin and mucosal membranes. Nikolsky sign is positive when gentle lateral pressure or rubbing of the skin causes the epidermis to shear away from the underlying dermis, resulting in skin peeling or blister extension. Histopathologic examination shows acantholysis, intradermal vesicle formation, and deposition of IgG.

topics.title: Bullous pemphigoid
topics.summary: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes along the basement membrane of the dermal-epi…

blocks.text: Etiology, Genetics & Risk Factors

Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes along the basement membrane of the dermal-epidermal junction. This causes the entire epidermis to separate from the dermis and form tense, subepidermal blisters.

Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disease that typically occurs in patients >60. It presents with tense bullae with rare mucosal involvement. Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes create subepidermal cleavage. Immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of IgG and/or C3 along the basement membrane (Deposition of IgG and complement at the dermal-epidermal junction).
Autoantibodies against hemidesmosome components initiate an inflammatory response that results in separation of the epidermis from the dermis, leading to subepidermal blisters.

blocks.text: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders characterized by epithelial fragility (eg, bullae, erosions, ulcers) triggered by minor trauma. It is caused by mutations affecting proteins in the intraepidermal and dermoepidermal adhesion complexes; keratin mutations (Impaired keratin filament assembly) are responsible for the most common form (EB simplex).

topics.summary: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by erythematous pruritic papules, vesicles, and bullae that appear symmet…

blocks.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis — Diagnosis, Histology

Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by erythematous pruritic papules, vesicles, and bullae that appear symmetrically on extensor surfaces. It is strongly associated with celiac disease, a disorder characterized histologically by small intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and villous atrophy.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is a vesiculobullous disorder characterized by small, tense vesicles located on extensor sites (elbows, knees, and buttocks), which are extremely pruritic. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) demonstrates a granular pattern of IgA deposition along the basement membrane at the tips of the dermal papillae. Dermatitis herpetiformis has a strong association with celiac disease, or gluten-sensitive enteropathy, and the primary treatment is the avoidance of gluten. In severe presentations, dapsone can be used to provide near immediate relief.

DH is characterized histologically by microabscesses containing fibrin and neutrophils at the dermal papillae tips. The overlying basal cells become vacuolated, and coalescing blisters form at the tips of the involved papillae. Immunofluorescent imaging shows deposition of IgA at the dermoepidermal junction.

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

This patient's rash is consistent with erythema multiforme (EM), an acute inflammatory disorder that can involve the skin of the extremities, face, trunk, and neck. Severe cases (EM major) can also affect oral mucous membranes and the tongue. Erythema multiforme is a cell-mediated inflammatory disorder of the skin characterized by erythematous papules that evolve into target lesions. It is most commonly associated with herpes simplex virus.

This patient's target-shaped skin lesions likely indicate erythema multiforme (EM), an acute, inflammatory skin disorder that usually develops in the setting of an ongoing infection. Although herpes simplex virus is the most common trigger, respiratory tract infections due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae (eg, low-grade fever, headache, fatigue, cough, wheezes) frequently cause EM in children. It is caused by the deposition of infectious antigens in keratinocytes, leading to a strong cell-mediated (eg, cytotoxic T-cell) immune response.

blocks.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome — Clinical Presentation

Lamotrigine can be used to treat partial and generalized seizures and works by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are rare, life-threatening adverse effects characterized by flu-like symptoms followed by widespread mucocutaneous epidermal necrosis. The first appearance of rash requires discontinuation of the drug immediately as SJS/TEN and benign rash cannot be distinguished reliably. Other anticonvulsants associated with SJS/TEN include carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and phenytoin.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome is characterized by rapid onset of erythematous macules with necrosis and skin sloughing. Systemic signs (eg, fever, hypotension) are common. Stevens-Johnson syndrome may also cause target lesions, but it is usually associated with medications (eg, sulfonamides, allopurinol, phenytoin).

topics.title: Dress Syndrome
topics.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome typically occurs 2-8 weeks after exposure to…

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome typically occurs 2-8 weeks after exposure to high-risk drugs such as anticonvulsants (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, sulfonamides (eg, sulfasalazine), and antibiotics (eg, minocycline, vancomycin). Patients typically develop fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, facial edema, diffuse skin rash, eosinophilia, and internal organ dysfunction.

topics.summary: Cutaneous warts (ie, verruca vulgaris) are caused by human papillomavirus and typically present as rough, skin-colo…

blocks.text: Cutaneous warts (ie, verruca vulgaris)

Cutaneous warts (ie, verruca vulgaris) are caused by human papillomavirus and typically present as rough, skin-colored papules. If necessary, biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and shows epidermal hyperplasia, thickened stratum corneum, papilloma formation, and cytoplasmic vacuolization.

This patient has cutaneous warts (verruca vulgaris), presenting as painless, skin-colored papules with a dry, whitish surface. The diagnosis of cutaneous warts is usually made on inspection, although a magnified view (ie, dermatoscopy) can be helpful and typically reveals small black dots representing thrombosed capillaries. Cutaneous warts are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), which is also the cause of plantar warts and anogenital warts (ie, condyloma acuminata).

blocks.text: Etiology, Genetics & Risk Factors
Impetigo

Bullous impetigo is a superficial infection by Staphylococcus aureus that is most common in young children. It is characterized by a blistering skin rash with tan- to honey-colored crusts. The blistering in bullous impetigo is caused by exfoliative toxin A, which targets desmoglein 1 in epidermal cellular junctions and causes a loss of cell adhesion.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome occurs in infants and children due to the production of exfoliative exotoxins by Staphylococcus aureus. The toxins cleave desmoglein in desmosomes, leading to widespread epidermal blistering and shedding, especially with gentle pressure (ie, Nikolsky sign). Mucous membranes are spared. SSSS is most common in infants and young children, and skin findings are often preceded or accompanied by fever, irritability, malaise, and poor feeding. Treatment includes antistaphylococcal antibiotics (eg, nafcillin, oxacillin).
Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS)

This patient has hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), which is characterized by painful, deep-seated nodules and scar formation in the axillae, groin, and medial thighs. The pathogenesis of HS begins with the occlusion of folliculopilosebaceous units caused by keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation. HS is a chronic, recurring condition with progressive formation of draining abscesses, sinus tracts (formed by epithelial stem cells released from follicular rupture), comedones (from significant follicular damage), and extensive fibrosis. In contrast to common furuncles and carbuncles, which usually resolve completely with drainage and antibacterial therapy, HS may persist and recur despite months of antibiotic therapy.

blocks.text: Terbinafine — Pathophysiology

Tinea corporis presents with round or ovoid lesions with a raised, scaly border and central clearing. Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause and infects keratinized matter in the stratum corneum of the superficial epidermis but does not invade the dermis or subcutaneous tissues. (Microbial infection of keratinized structures)
Terbinafine is used for treatment of dermatophytosis. It inhibits synthesis of fungal membrane ergosterol by suppressing the enzyme squalene epoxidase.

blocks.text: Tinea pedis — Etiology, Genetics

Tinea pedis is a superficial infection of the epidermis caused by dermatophytes (eg, Trichophyton rubrum). It most often presents as a pruritic, erythematous rash between the toes that frequently extends along the sole. Microscopy of skin scrapings shows branching hyphae. Treatment options include a variety of topical antifungals (clotrimazole), but not nystatin. (see figure below)

blocks.text: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor)

Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is a superficial skin infection caused by Malassezia species. It causes erythematous, hyper- or hypopigmented macules and patches. Malassezia forms spores and hyphae, producing the characteristic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on KOH preparation light microscopy.

The eruption of multiple, nontender, and nonpruritic hypopigmented macules with fine scaling after traveling to a warm, humid climate raises suspicion for a diagnosis of pityriasis versicolor. Pityriasis versicolor is most commonly caused by increased growth of Malassezia globosa or other fungi of the Malassezia genus (e.g., Malassezia furfur), which belong to the physiological flora of the skin.

blocks.text: Pigmented skin disorders — Clinical Principles (Part 1)

Melanin is a pigment made by melanocytes within a specialized cellular organelle called a melanosome. The number of melanosomes (not melanocytes) and density of melanin are what provide variation in skin tone.
Oculocutaneous albinism

Oculocutaneous albinism is most commonly due to mutations that cause dysfunctional melanin synthesis within melanosomes. Patients typically have complete absence of melanin, resulting in white skin and hair, light irides, photophobia, and a propensity for sunburns. In addition to pigmentation, melanin plays a role in guiding embryologic development of ocular structures. Without melanin, patients have misrouted and underdeveloped optic nerve fibers and hypoplastic or absent foveae, as seen in this infant. This leads to findings of decreased visual acuity and, in turn, strabismus (ie, ocular misalignment) and/or nystagmus.

Oculocutaneous albinism is an autosomal recessive disorder of melanin biosynthesis typically due to defective tyrosinase activity. Patients have reduced or absent melanin pigment in the skin, hair, and eye, as well as abnormal development of the fovea and optic nerve fibers, leading to reduced visual acuity and nystagmus.
Vitiligo

Vitiligo is a common condition characterized by the loss of epidermal melanocytes. It occurs more commonly in patients with autoimmune disorders (eg, autoimmune thyroiditis, type I diabetes) and results in well-defined, variably sized patches of hypopigmentation. The pathogenesis of vitiligo is multifactorial but likely involves CD8+ lymphocyte–mediated melanocyte apoptosis.
Waardenburg syndrome

Waardenburg syndrome is a syndrome of patchy depigmentation of the skin, hair, irises, and cochlear dysfunction that results from a defect in the differentiation of neural crest cells into melanocytes. Patients typically present with a white forelock and eyelashes, depigmented skin patches, iridic heterochromia, and sensorineural hearing loss.

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

B henselae can also cause bacillary angiomatosis (BA) in immunocompromised patients. BA presents with red-purple papular skin lesions. These vascular proliferations may also be found within the viscera. BA can be fatal if left untreated.

topics.summary: This patient's small, bright-red, papular lesions are cherry hemangiomas, also known as cherry angiomas or senile h…

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

This patient's small, bright-red, papular lesions are cherry hemangiomas, also known as cherry angiomas or senile hemangiomas. They are the most common benign vascular tumors in adults and typically appear during the third or fourth decade of life. The lesions do not regress spontaneously and often multiply with age. Cherry hemangiomas are always superficial on the skin and are not found on the mucosa or deep tissues. Histologically, they appear as sharply circumscribed areas of congested capillaries and post-capillary venules in the papillary dermis.

blocks.text: Pathophysiology & Mechanism

A benign glomus tumor (glomangioma) can produce a very tender, small (a few millimeters in diameter), red-blue lesion under the nail bed. This type of tumor originates from the modified smooth muscle cells that control the thermoregulatory functions of dermal glomus bodies.

blocks.text: Kaposi sarcoma — Etiology, Genetics

Oral thrush (eg, white buccal and palatal plaques) and bilateral tender lymphadenopathy in a patient with a history of intravenous drug use are highly suggestive of HIV infection. HIV is further supported by the presence of Kaposi sarcoma (KS), a vascular tumor common in HIV-positive individuals and an AIDS-defining malignancy. KS is strongly associated with human herpesvirus type 8 (HHV-8), as well as an impaired T-cell response (eg, HIV infection).

This patient with a history of HIV infection and a current CD4 count of 100/mm3 now has 2 lesions on the right thigh that are violaceous, raised, and nontender. This presentation is classic for Kaposi sarcoma (KS), It is a vascular tumor caused by human herpesvirus type 8 infection of endothelial cells.

Kaposi sarcoma is a low-grade neoplasm of the vascular endothelial cells, which is characterized clinically by violaceous or reddish-purple patches, plaques, or tumors. Histologic examination demonstrates slit-like vascular spaces surrounded by a proliferation of spindle cells. It is typically caused by HHV-8.

Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors composed of proliferating endothelial cells that most frequently affect the head or neck region. Natural history of these lesions involves rapid growth of a red, cutaneous plaque followed by spontaneous regression.

Infantile hemangioma is a common, benign vascular tumor that presents soon after birth as a bright red, raised, sharply demarcated plaque. The natural course of hemangiomas is proliferation in infancy followed by regression in early childhood.

topics.summary: This patient has varicose veins and edema in the lower extremities consistent with chronic venous insufficiency. Ve…

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

This patient has varicose veins and edema in the lower extremities consistent with chronic venous insufficiency. Venous insufficiency is a multifactorial process; contributing factors include obstruction of venous return (eg, pregnancy, obesity), increased orthostatic pressure (eg, prolonged standing), decreased muscular compression (eg, sedentary lifestyle), and damaged venous valves (eg, due to deep vein thrombosis).

Chronic venous insufficiency develops due to venous hypertension, which can lead to venous dilation and venous valve dysfunction, allowing retrograde venous flow. The subsequent pooling of venous blood increases local hydrostatic pressure, resulting in lower extremity edema that may be unilateral (eg, early disease course) or bilateral.

Over time, patients with venous insufficiency can develop extravasation of fluid, plasma proteins, and red cells, leading to chronic inflammation and stasis dermatitis (SD). SD is characterized by erythema, induration, fibrosis, and deposition of hemosiderin (from breakdown of extravasated RBCs) manifesting as reddish-brown discoloration, as in this patient. Symptoms are typically bilateral and usually worse at or above the ankles. Complications of SD include poor wound healing and ulceration.
Stasis dermatitis — Clinical Presentation

Chronically elevated venous pressure in the lower extremities can lead to incompetent venous valves and venous dilation (varicose veins). Venous congestion and tissue ischemia can result in venous stasis dermatitis.

Stasis dermatitis is a classic manifestation of chronic venous insufficiency and presents with reddish-brown ankle discoloration and induration. These effects are caused by cellular extravasation from dilated veins and dermal fibrosis.(see figure below)

Neuropathic foot ulcers can occur in diabetic patients when loss of pain sensation and proprioception delays recognition of injury due to trauma, friction, or sustained pressure (on plantar surface of foot bones). The risk is greatest in patients with longstanding diabetes who have poor glycemic control.

Acanthosis nigricans presents with thickening and hyperpigmentation of skin in the flexural areas. The lesions have a classic "velvety" texture. Acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with insulin-resistant states (eg, diabetes mellitus, acromegaly, obesity) and gastrointestinal malignancies.

Septal panniculitis containing granulomas with giant cells is characteristic of erythema nodosum (EN), a delayed hypersensitivity reaction associated with infectious, inflammatory, and autoimmune processes. EN typically causes smooth, tender pretibial nodules.

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation & Physical Exam

Melanocytic nevi are benign neoplasms composed of round, uniform melanocytes (nevus cells) that are mitotically quiescent. Melanocytic nevi are progressive lesions that typically mature through the following phases:

Junctional nevi are characterized by aggregates of nevus cells limited to the dermoepidermal junction. They typically appear as flat, black to brown macules with darker color in the center than in the periphery and preserved skin markings.

Compound nevi form as the aggregates of nevus cells extend into the dermis. They are raised papules with uniform brown to tan pigmentation. This patient's lesion is a compound nevus because it has both dermal and epidermal involvement.

Intradermal nevi are older lesions in which the epidermal nests of nevus cells have been lost. The remaining dermal nevus cells lose tyrosinase activity and produce little to no pigment. Intradermal nevi are often skin-colored, dome-shaped, and sometimes pedunculated.

Seborrheic keratosis is a common epidermal tumor that presents as a tan or brown, round lesion with a well-demarcated border and "stuck-on" appearance. Microscopic examination shows small cells resembling basal cells, with pigmentation, hyperkeratosis, and keratin-containing cysts. Rapid onset of numerous lesions is often associated with internal malignancy (Leser-Trélat sign).

blocks.text: Etiology, Genetics & Risk Factors

Imiquimod is a topical immunomodulatory drug that is used to treat many common dermatologic disorders associated with abnormal cell proliferation, including anogenital warts (ie, human papillomavirus infection), superficial basal cell carcinoma, and actinic keratosis. The antiviral and antiproliferative effects of imiquimod are primarily mediated through activation of toll-like receptor 7, which upregulates the proinflammatory transcription factor nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB).
Urticaria

Urticaria is a transient hypersensitivity disorder characterized by pruritic erythematous plaques that arise suddenly and resolve over hours. They are most often caused by IgE-mediated degranulation of mast cells, leading to increased permeability of the microvasculature with edema of the superficial dermis.

A number of medications, including opioids, radiocontrast agents, and some antibiotics (eg, vancomycin), can trigger IgE-independent mast cell degranulation. Common symptoms include diffuse itching and pain, bronchospasm, and localized swelling (urticaria).
Ecchymoses

Ecchymoses frequently indicate a deep hemorrhage (hematoma) due to bony fracture, ligamentous rupture, or muscular injury. They do not blanch under pressure as the red blood cells are not contained within the vasculature. Ecchymoses often pass through an evolution of color change (blue or red to brown, green, and yellow), which can be used to estimate the age of the injury.(see figure below)

blocks.text: Late-stage radiation dermatitis — Etiology, Genetics

This patient has a persistent, itchy, ulcerating skin lesion with hypopigmentation and telangiectasias at a site of prior radiotherapy, consistent with late-stage radiation dermatitis. Ionizing radiation causes apoptosis of rapidly dividing cancer cells directly by inducing DNA damage and indirectly by generating free radicals.

Late-stage radiation dermatitis occurs months to years after radiation exposure and is characterized grossly by pigment changes, telangiectasias, and chronic ulceration. Typical histologic changes include vascular abnormalities, fibroblast proliferation, and homogenization of dermal collagen (ie, fibrosis) due to the increased expression of transforming growth factor-beta.

This patient has erythema that blanches without blistering, which is characteristic of a superficial burn. Burn wounds are classified according to depth based on which layers of cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues are damaged:

The earliest morphologic change that occurs after a superficial thermal burn is erythema due to the release of preformed mediators (eg, histamine) from mast cells. Deeper (eg, partial-thickness) burn wounds form blisters due to fluid extravasation through gaps between damaged venule endothelial cells.
Hypermetabolic response in burn injury

Patients with severe burn injury commonly develop a hypermetabolic response that results in an increased basal metabolic rate and, often, lean muscle wasting. Administration of oxandrolone, a synthetic testosterone analogue, enhances muscle protein synthesis and decreases protein catabolism, reducing lean muscle loss.

Severe partial- or full-thickness burns cause insensible fluid losses because of impaired epidermal barriers, and they require intensive fluid resuscitation. Burns also cause a hypermetabolic state and patients have an increased nutritional requirement.

topics.summary: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer and is derived from the basal cells of the epidermis.

blocks.text: Basal cell carcinoma — Diagnosis, Histology
Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer and is derived from the basal cells of the epidermis.

Basal cell carcinomas arise from keratinocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis or hair follicle (Epidermal keratinocytes). They most commonly occur on the face and often appear as pearly or translucent, pink or skin-colored papules with central telangiectatic vessels.

Biopsy classically shows nests of basaloid keratinocytes with peripheral palisading and clefting artifact. Unresected BCCs rarely metastasize but may undergo continued local growth, causing progressive surrounding tissue destruction.

blocks.text: This patient's persistent skin lesion in a sun-exposed area (eg, ear) is concerning for skin cancer, particularly basal cell carcinoma (BCC) or cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Both BCC and cutaneous SCC, which are composed of malignant keratinocytes, can present as a skin-colored nodule. Sometimes differences in gross appearance and texture can help distinguish between the two neoplasms:
Nodular BCC classically has a translucent or pearly appearance, often with central telangiectasias.
Cutaneous SCC classically has a rough or scaly (keratinized) surface.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) classically presents as a rough or scaly (keratinized) nodule. Diagnosis is made with biopsy, which typically reveals nests of dysplastic keratinocytes with eosinophilic cytoplasm (due to keratin filaments). Dermal involvement signifies invasive SCC.

Microscopy of this patient's enlarging, crusted skin lesion reveals invasive nests of atypical cells surrounding keratin pearls, which is consistent with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Although risk of cutaneous SCC is increased by solar damage, chronic inflammation, and ionizing radiation, the primary driver of malignancy in this patient is likely the use of immunosuppressive medications (eg, tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone).
Actinic keratoses (AKs)

This patient's forehead lesions are characteristic of actinic keratoses (AKs), which are small, scaly, erythematous lesions with a sandpaper texture occurring on sun-exposed areas. On light microscopy, AKs show hyperkeratosis (hyperplasia of the stratum corneum), parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum), and atypical keratinocytes with pleomorphic nuclei and multiple mitoses. There may also be pigment irregularities and dilated blood vessels affecting the surrounding skin, which are consistent with chronic sun exposure.

AKs do not invade the dermis and are considered to be premalignant lesions. Over several years, a small percentage of AKs transform into invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), a change reflected by an increase in lesion size and thickness, dermal invasion, and metastatic potential.

Actinic keratosis (see figure below) is a premalignant lesion, which may progress to squamous cell carcinoma and is typically seen in areas of prolonged sun exposure. Lesions clinically appear as light pink, ill-defined macules with a gritty texture.
Dysplasia of keratinocytes leading to the development of actinic keratoses is the most likely cause of multiple, asymptomatic, ill-defined scaly lesions on sun-exposed sites of this older patient.

Diagnosis, Histology & Laboratory Findings
The most common metastatic tumors to the brain are lung cancer, renal cancer, and melanoma. Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes, which are embryologically derived from neural crest cells.
BRAF is a protein kinase involved in activation of signaling pathways for melanocyte proliferation; the BRAF V600E mutation is seen in 40%-60% of patients with melanoma.
Melanoma is often diagnosed when immunostaining of biopsy samples reveals multiple melanocyte markers (eg, S-100, HMB-45, MART-1).

Melanoma often has an early horizontal growth phase with low metastatic potential followed by a nodular, vertical growth phase with a significantly increased risk of metastasis. Depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) is the most important prognostic indicator in malignant melanoma.
Embryology, Anatomy & Normal Physiology

Melanoma lesions often have multiple color variations. The different colors represent different activities within the tumor. Whitish/gray areas occur when cytotoxic T cells recognize tumor antigens and destroy malignant cells, leading to melanocyte regression. Red areas arise due to vessel ectasia and local inflammation, whereas brown or black areas are generally due to advancing malignant melanocytes.
Melanocyte regression is also a hallmark of treatment response to melanoma immunotherapies, such as the programmed cell death receptor-1 (PD-1) inhibitor pembrolizumab.

Lentigo maligna is a subtype of malignant melanoma that most commonly manifests on the sun-exposed skin of elderly patients. It is often slow growing and typically confined to the dermal-epidermal junction.

Acral lentiginous melanoma is a subtype of melanoma that occurs on the distal extremities (acral sites> Palms). Its development is not associated with UV radiation, and it is the most common subtype of melanoma in individuals with darker skin.
Pathophysiology & Mechanism

A 65-year-old man comes to the office due to 2 months of fatigue and persistent, nonproductive cough. He has a history of coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction. Three years ago, he underwent wide local excision of a melanoma on his posterior neck. The patient has a 50-pack-year smoking history. Vital signs are within normal limits. Chest radiograph reveals multiple lung lesions and hilar lymphadenopathy. Histopathology from one of the biopsied lung lesions is shown below after staining with hematoxylin and eosin > Metastatic melanoma

Aldesleukin is recombinant interleukin-2 (IL-2), a cytokine that is secreted by all T-cell subtypes. IL-2 triggers the destruction of tumor cells via the activation of cell types that recognize MHC I receptors. IL-2 stimulates the activation of natural killer cells (NK cells) and cytotoxic T cells. These activated cells recognize the absence of MHC I receptors on infected or malignant cells and consequently destroy them. Aldesleukin is used in the therapy of both metastatic melanoma and renal cell carcinoma.

Programmed-death receptor 1 (PD-1) is a checkpoint inhibitor that downregulates the cytotoxic T-cell response. Neoplastic cells often exploit this receptor via the overexpression of PD-1 ligand. PD-1 receptor inhibitors (eg, Pembrolizumab) restore the T-cell response, allowing cytotoxic T cells to invade the tumor and induce apoptosis of neoplastic cells.

rapidFireQAs.a: seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff); treatment = topical selenium or ketoconazole shampoo; does not cause circular area of alopecia as with tinea capitis; more common in adults (tinea capitis more common in children); cause is inflammatory response to over- colonization with Malassezia yeast. rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + white, cheese-like discharge per vaginum; Q asks what oral treatment she needs; answer = fluconazole; some students say, “Wait, I thought we use topical nystatin”

rapidFireQAs.a: Tx for tinea pedis on USMLE is topical terbinafine or -azole (i.e., clotrimazole/miconazole).

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + diabetic foot ulcer; sterile probe to base of lesion is likely to show what?
rapidFireQAs.a: correct answer on new NBME exam = “polymicrobial”; wrong answers are Staph aureus and Pseudomonas. This is an extremely important Q from NBME because people have long debated Staph vs Pseudomonas for diabetic foot ulcers.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60M + farmer + thickened yellow nailbed of left big toe; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: onychomycosis (fungus of nails); Tx = oral terbinafine (if not listed, choose griseofulvin).

rapidFireQAs.a: lymphangitis; diagnosis is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii); this image of erythematous lesions streaking toward the axilla is exceedingly HY for lymphangitis; sometimes the image can just be a fine pink streak without open lesions. Wrong answers are phlebitis, arteritis; treatment is oral itraconazole. rapidFireQAs.a: Candida (diaper rash); not atopic dermatitis; the latter can occur in babies but is more often on trunk, dorsa of hands, and face. Treat Candida diaper rash with topical -azoles or nystatin.

rapidFireQAs.a: oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or Augmentin (amoxicillin + clavulanate); diagnosis is cellulitis (infection of the dermis and hypodermis [subcutaneous fat]); Staph aureus exceeds Strep pyogenes (Group A Strep) as causal organism; must give beta-lactamase-resistant beta- lactam in the methicillin class (i.e., dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin) or first-generation cephalosporin (i.e., cephalexin, cephazolin), or Augmentin (amoxicillin-clavulanate); amoxicillin and penicillin alone are wrong answers; 90% of community Staph (i.e., MSSA) produces beta-lactamase, so amoxicillin and penicillin alone will not work if Staph is the cause.

Although Group A Strep > Staph for erysipelas, Tx is same as cellulitis (oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or Augmentin) because Staph can still cause it. Penicillin alone can be used for Strep pharyngitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + cellulitis + BP of 80/40; Q asks which immunologic receptor(s) is/are bound in this patient’s condition → answer = MHC-II and T-cell receptor; diagnosis is toxic shock-like syndrome caused by exotoxin A (erythrogenic toxin) of Strep pyogenes (Group A Strep); mechanism is similar to Staph aureus superantigen, TSST, which bridges MHC-II on macrophages and TCR, causing cytokine release from macrophages.
rapidFireQAs.a: Toxic shock syndrome Qs will mention low BP in someone with cotton nasal packing or tampons → answer is “MHC-II and TCR” bound by TSST of Staph aureus. In contrast, cellulitis causing shock, the answer will be Strep pyogenes (Staph will not be listed) due to its exotoxin A.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12F + fever + sore throat + red tongue + pink maculopapular body rash; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: scarlet fever caused by Strep pyogenes; presents with “strawberry tongue” and salmon-pink body rash; Tx with penicillin to prevent rheumatic heart disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14M + fever + rapid, irregular, jerking movements of limbs + following rash on legs as shown; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: erythema marginatum as seen in rheumatic fever; treatment is penicillin; erythema marginatum is annular (ring-like) and serpiginous (serpent-/snake-like); movements are Sydenham chorea (autoimmune attack against basal ganglia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 10M + “yellow crusties” on his forearm for the past week + red urine; what’s the diagnosis? → answer = post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) secondary to Strep impetigo. USMLE can sometimes write answer as “proliferative glomerulonephritis” or “acute glomerulonephritis.” This is a type-III hypersensitivity with immune complex deposition in the kidney. USMLE loves PSGN due to cutaneous Strep (i.e., PSGN need not be caused by Strep pharyngitis).
rapidFireQAs.a: Proliferative glomerulonephritis = PSGN. Do not confuse this with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (DPGN, which is red urine in SLE), or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN, which is red urine in HepC or malignancy).

rapidFireQAs.q: 19M + burned leg playing with firecrackers + while in hospital develops infection of burn site that has a yellow color; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus (golden staph); wrong answer is Pseudomonas. Although this is HY organism in burns patients, it produces a blue-green color due to pyocyanin, not a yellow color, which is instead golden Staph. So USMLE likes to be tricky that way.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + breastfeeding + red, cracked, fissured nipple; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mastitis; usually caused by Staph aureus; Tx is oral dicloxacillin + continue breastfeeding through the affected breast.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + recently stopped breastfeeding + tender, fluctuant mass lateral to the nipple; patient is afebrile; mass is not warm or red; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: galactocele (milk retention cyst); can sometimes be confused with abscess since it is fluctuant and can be tender; if abscess, however, they will say red/warm +/- fever.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + inverted nipple + patient is worried because family Hx of breast cancer; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ductal ectasia; benign condition; as name implies, simply dilation/widening of lactiferous duct.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + red, eczematoid-appearing nipple + mass palpable beneath nipple; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Paget disease of breast; often associated with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + peau d’orange of left breast + erythematous; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: inflammatory breast cancer; peau d’orange appearance due to Coopers ligaments of breast (on NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + presents as per image shown; what’s the diagnosis? (answers are either Propionibacterium acnes or tinea faciei):
rapidFireQAs.a: acne; Propionibacterium acnes; not difficult, but I’ve seen enough students select tinea faciei. First-line Tx for acne on USMLE is topical retinoids (i.e., topical tretinoin; not oral isotretinoin; latter is only for severe acne). Topical retinoids (vitamin A) inhibit sebum production; they cause photosensitivity and desquamation (peeling). Topical benzoyl peroxide is second-line for acne (although often co-administered with topical tretinoin). It clears pores and kills bacteria. Topical clindamycin can be used if topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide are insufficient; if topical antibiotic is insufficient, oral tetracycline is used; the latter causes blistering photosensitivity. Last resort is oral isotretinoin; must do beta-hCG (pregnancy test) before commencement due to teratogenicity; oral isotretinoin does not cause problems with sperm in men; topical retinoids in both men and women do not cause teratogenicity.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + being treated for acne with both topical + oral medications; her forehead is shown below; what is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: “avoidance of sun exposure”; above rash is classic photosensitivity caused by topical retinoids; tetracycline photosensitivity tends to be blistering; do not choose answers such as “avoidance of spicy/sweet foods” for acne questions.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + face shown in following image; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is tinea faciei; Tx = topical -azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + fever of 103 F + stiff neck + low BP; following image of patient’s leg is shown. What is the most likely causal organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: gram-negative diplococci; Dx is meningitis + characteristic non-blanching rash caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Low BP can be endotoxic shock, but student should bear in mind Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is often asked; give hydrocortisone to increase BP after normal saline is administered. WHF syndrome = bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis of the adrenal cortices caused by meningococcal septicemia → low aldosterone + low cortisol.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + 2-day Hx of soreness of left knee and right elbow + positive Finkelstein test on right hand + cutaneous papules visualized on right wrist; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: gonococcal arthritis; will present one of two ways on USMLE; 1) monoarthritis of large joint, such as the knee; 2) polyarthritis + tenosynovitis (e.g., deQuervain) + cutaneous papules/vesicopustules. The USMLE will sometimes just have “gram- negative diplococcus” as the answer. Finkelstein test is an MSK exam maneuver to diagnose deQuervain tenosynovitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + penetrating trauma to thigh one week ago + skin has black appearance and crepitus on exam; the most likely causal organism can also cause what?
rapidFireQAs.a: watery diarrhea; Dx is gas gangrene due to Clostridium perfringens, resulting in subcutaneous emphysema (crunching of skin due to underlying CO2 gas); this is due to production of lecithinase (phospholipase); C. perfringens also causes watery diarrhea.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56F + poorly controlled diabetes + Pseudomonal sepsis + following image is shown; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ecthyma gangrenosum; uncommon cutaneous infection seen in patients with severe Pseudomonal infections.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + works as postal worker + horticulturist + has many pet birds; following image is shown + Q describes lesion as an eschar with surrounding edema; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Bacillus anthracis (anthrax); cutaneous anthrax can present classically with a black, eschar lesion; the gram (+) rod increases cAMP and produces edema factor.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F gives birth to stillborn neonate + she ate soft cheeses and deli meat while pregnant + stillborn has diffuse granulomas on body; which of the following best describes the most likely causal organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: gram (+) rods; Listeria can cause granulomatosis infantiseptica (severe intrauterine infection often resulting in fetal demise + diffuse cutaneous granulomas).

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + bilateral pneumonia + skin ulcer on back of hand (image shown) + low-grade fever + has many pet rabbits; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Francisella tularensis; cutaneous tularemia can present as ulcerative lesions; can also cause bilateral atypical pneumonia; rabbits are classic source.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + type II diabetic + red rash under right axilla + rash appears bright coral red under Woods lamp (image shown); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum; skin infection of intertriginous areas that shines/glows coral red (holy shit) under Woods lamp.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + painful erythematous lesions in her axillae; an image is shown below; what’s the best treatment for this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME answer = “surgical excision of lesions”; diagnosis is hidradenitis suppurativa, a skin condition characterized by painful abscesses and sinus tracts, most commonly in the groin, axilla, and under the breasts; frequently affects apocrine glands; cause is a combination of genetic and environmental factors (idiopathic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + athlete + strong body odor when finished with sports; Q asks what type of gland is responsible → answer = apocrine; Types of glands:
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants you to know apocrine glands are found in the groin and axilla and are responsible for body odor. Part of the plasma membrane buds off with the substance secreted by the cell. “Apocrine metaplasia,” is a term sometimes applied to fibrocystic change of the breast (as well as “blue dome cysts” and “sclerosing adenosis”). Eccrine (merocrine) glands are simple sweat glands found all over the body. The secreted substance is merely exocytosed from the cell. Sebaceous glands (holocrine) are those attached to hair follicles (not found on palms/soles). The cell disintegrates when it secretes the substance.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + recent penetrating trauma to leg + necrotic tissue that on examination appears to spread along fascial planes; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: necrotizing fasciitis; Tx = IV antibiotics + debridement of necrotic tissue.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + painful 1-cm lump in labia majora; what’s the most likely causal organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymicrobial; diagnosis is Bartholin gland cyst/abscess; uncomplicated cysts → treatment = warm compresses or sitz bath; overt abscess → Tx answer = drainage.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + fever for 5 days + palms and soles desquamation + edema of dorsa of hands + cervical lymphadenopathy + injection of conjunctiva and lips; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Kawasaki disease; 5+ days of fever is HY; Tx = aspirin + IVIG (never give aspirin to kids for other purposes because of Reye syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + lives in Connecticut + went hiking five days ago + rash of wrists and ankles + rash migrates in toward chest; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii); classically palms and soles rash, but USMLE also sometimes says wrists + ankles; student should be aware rash is centripetal (i.e., starts at palms/soles, or wrists/ankles, and moves inward to trunk); treatment is doxycycline for anyone age 9 and older; pregnant women and children 8 and younger receive other agents, such as amoxicillin or ceftriaxone.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + vesicular eruption on bottoms of feet, palms, and periorally; most likely causal organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: “RNA virus; non-enveloped; non-segmented”; diagnosis is hand-foot-mouth disease caused by Coxsackie A virus; this virus can also cause herpangina (posterior oropharyngeal vesicles).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + recently returned home from military service + fever of 101 F + cervical lymphadenopathy + posterior oropharyngeal vesicles + painful vesicles inside the lip (nothing on outside of mouth/lips); Q asks next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: “PCR testing of vesicles”; viral culture is wrong answer; diagnosis is HSV1/2; do not confuse with herpangina; HSV primary infection will classically present with fever and lymphadenopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54F + image shown below; Q asks most likely organism in terms of viral structure (i.e., DNA vs RNA; enveloped vs non-enveloped; circular vs linear):
rapidFireQAs.a: DNA, enveloped, linear; Dx is HSV1/2; herpes labialis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + works as dentist + image as shown below; what’s the MOA of the treatment?
rapidFireQAs.a: Treatment = DNA polymerase inhibitor (causes “chain termination”); acyclovir (or valacyclovir); Dx is herpetic whitlow, which is an HSV1/2 infection of the finger, often caused by inoculation from a cold sore; increased prevalence in dentists/hygienists.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + gardener + photo is shown; this is due to what type of toxicity?
rapidFireQAs.a: NBME answer = arsenic; Mees lines are white lines seen on fingernails in arsenic toxicity; arsenic is present in small amounts in fertilizers, which causes plants to flourish; gardeners + landscapers at increased risk; arsenic can also cause palms/soles rash (arsenical keratosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + recent paranasal sinus infection + now presents with fever 103 F + painful, swollen eye as shown below; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is orbital cellulitis (infection involving tissues posterior to orbital septum); Staph aureus most common cause; rare sequela of adjacent infection, e.g., from the paranasal sinus; medical emergency; requires IV antibiotics; preseptal cellulitis is a less severe version of orbital cellulitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + painful, red bump on upper eyelid; image shown; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is hordeolum (stye); Staph aureus infection of sweat gland or oil duct; treat with warm compresses.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + painless ulcer on his penile shaft; Dx + Tx? → answer = primary syphilis (chancre sore described); organism is Treponema pallidum; diagnose with darkfield microscopy to visualize spirochetes; Tx with penicillin.
rapidFireQAs.a: Do not confuse with chancroid, which is a painful ulcer caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + Hx of unprotected intercourse + rash as shown in image below; KOH prep is negative; Q asks what is most likely to confirm diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer on USMLE = fluorescent treponemal antibody(FTA); Dx is secondary syphilis showing characteristic maculopapular/nodular body rash; negative KOH means it's not tinea versicolor; palms and soles are classically affected in secondary syphilis but Q need not mention it as per above. It's the negative KOH where you say, "Well if it's not tinea versicolor, what other DDx could it be? "Secondary syphilis is diagnosed with serology; Q need not mention Hx of chancre from primary syphilis. VDRL/RPR ordered before FTA, but latter more specific. Former can be falsely positive in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome (classically SLE patients with lupus anticoagulant). USMLE Q can also show you picture of wart-like lesions on the genitals (condylomata lata) + tell you there’s palms/soles rash, then answer = Treponema pallidum; this is also secondary syphilis presentation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + Hx of unprotected intercourse + recently immigrated to US from Egypt + presents with below image of lesion on forehead + 2/6 decrescendo holo-diastolic murmur auscultated on exam; the most likely causal organism bears taxonomy most similar to which of the following:
rapidFireQAs.a: Leptospira interrogans; diagnosis in image above is gumma of tertiary syphilis; syphilis is a spirochete, as are Leptospira, Borellia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), and Borrelia recurrentis (relapsing fever). Tertiary syphilis can cause ascending aortitis (murmur is AR).

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + from Massachusetts + family has pet dog + has rash as shown below; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Lyme disease; rash is erythema chronicum migrans (classic target rash); the rash need not be a target on USMLE; it can merely be circular with no clearing; but the target is classic; USMLE can give two side by side images: 1) circular rash on limb that is not a target; 2) Bells palsy → student needs to infer this is Lyme disease even though rash isn’t a target. Treatment in this kid is amoxicillin, not doxycycline. Treatment is doxycycline for most cases of Lyme; doxycycline is not given to children age 8 and younger or to pregnant women (causes teeth discoloration); if pregnant or age 8 and younger, give amoxicillin. Be aware ceftriaxone can be given for severe Lyme that is disseminated, causing cardiac or cognitive dysfunction.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + pregnant + Bells palsy + target rash; Q asks for treatment (answers are steroids, doxycycline, ceftriaxone)
rapidFireQAs.a: ceftriaxone; doxycycline not given to pregnant women or children under age 8; student says, “Wait, but I thought you just said ceftriaxone is for severe Lyme; her presentation is simple” → Yes, I agree, ceftriaxone is classically for severe Lyme, but in this Q, they force you to choose it because we can’t give doxy; you need to be flexible in some cases (example on NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + sleeps with pet dog + tick found on the dog + circular rash on arm + blood smear shows phagocytes with intracellular berry cluster organisms; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ehrlichiosis (Ehrlichia chaffeensis); bacterium spread by Ixodes tick (same as Lyme disease, Babesia, and Anaplasma); will not cause target rash; “berry cluster organisms” or intracellular “morulae” may be seen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + living in homeless shelter for past 4 months + itchy hands + image shown below + topical antifungals were attempted but not effective; Q asks for the treatment:
rapidFireQAs.a: topical permethrin; Dx is scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei); lesions classically described as “linear burrows”; can become superinfected with Staph aureus. Disseminated scabies can occur in HIV patients; Tx is oral ivermectin. Topical permethrin is also treatment for pediculosis (lice).

rapidFireQAs.q: 19F + recent travel through southern US + stayed at dodgy AF motel on the side of the highway next to a Denny’s and a Sonic + itchy lesions on arm as shown in image below; Q asks for organism:
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer on NBME = bed bugs; caused by an insect called Cimex.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + family recently immigrated to US from Albania + diffuse maculopapular rash + photograph of buccal mucosa is shown below; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = measles (rubeola); Tx is supportive; image shows Koplik spots (pathognomonic whiteish lesions on buccal mucosa); immigrant Hx on USMLE sometimes implies unvaccinated status.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + diffuse maculopapular rash + tenderness at base of occiput and behind the ears; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is rubella (German measles); Tx is supportive; suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy are characteristic.

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + fever + image shown below; what is the most likely causal organism (DNA vs RNA; enveloped vs non-enveloped; segmented vs non-segmented)?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is mumps → causes POM → Parotitis, Orchitis, Meningitis; virus is RNA, enveloped, non- segmented.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + hepatomegaly + rash as shown in image below; no murmurs; Q asks most likely causal organism:
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV); image shows blueberry muffin rash; no murmurs implies not rubella (causes patent ductus arteriosus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 5M + fever 2-3 days ago + brought in by mother to emergency with appearance as shown below; the most likely causal organism can also cause what?
rapidFireQAs.a: aplastic anemia; Dx = Parvovirus B19 (Fifth disease); image shows classic “slapped cheek” appearance; next best step in Dx = Parvovirus B19 IgM titers. If IgM titers are not listed and the child has aplastic anemia, choose bone marrow biopsy. If the patient doesn't have aplastic anemia, you don't need to do the biopsy. There is increased risk of aplastic anemia in sickle cell, but not mandatory the child has that. Once child has developed the red cheeks, he/she has immunologically cleared the illness (i.e., if they turn it into a communications style Q, tell parents to relax because the child has cleared the virus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + works at daycare center + fever + rash as shown in image below; next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Parvovirus IgM titers. Viral infections in general can present with exanthem (rash). If they say "daycare center," this is hyper buzzy for Parvo on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + high school wrestler + Hx of atopy + has burning, painful rash on trunk + lymphadenopathy + fever; image shown below; Q asks what’s the treatment?
rapidFireQAs.a: oral acyclovir (or valacyclovir); diagnosis is eczema herpeticum → HSV1/2 infection superimposed on eczema; often self-inoculated from touching cold sore then cracked skin of eczema; herpes infection can present with fever, lymphadenopathy, and tingling, burning, and painful rash (herpetic neuralgia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + undergoing chemotherapy for ALL + has rash as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: shingles; yes, pediatric shingles “is a thing”; patient is immunocompromised due to chemotherapy. Shingles is aka “herpes zoster” and is caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV); herpes zoster is not a virus name; herpes zoster literally is just another name for shingles, which is caused by VZV (human herpes virus 3; HHV3), not HSV1/2 (HHV1/2).

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + immigrated to US from Mexico in elementary school + presents with crops of pruritic vesicles on the trunk at different stages of healing; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: varicella (chickenpox); immigrant status implies unvaccinated status; “crops of vesicles at different stages of healing” = buzzy for VZV.

rapidFireQAs.q: 2M + fever of 103-4 F for 3 days; fever abruptly subsides, followed by rash as shown below; patient’s vaccination Hx is up to date; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: roseola (HHV6); described as “spiking fever followed by a rash”; child will have high fever for 2-3 days, followed by a rash.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + no past medical history + afebrile + itchy rash on back for past week as shown below; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = pityriasis rosea; caused by HHV6 or 7; self-limiting; starts as Herald patch (larger pink ellipse above), usually on the back or trunk, then spreads upward onto the shoulder blades (“Christmas tree distribution”); USMLE will show you image and expect you can make spot- diagnosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + Hx of IV drug use + violaceous skin lesions as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Kaposi sarcoma; usually caused by HHV8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpes virus) in immunocompromised patients (i.e., AIDS, chemotherapy); Kaposi sarcoma presents as tumorous lesions of vascular-lymphatic origin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + undergoing chemotherapy for ALL + skin lesions as shown in image below; Q asks you to pick the organism that causes it, but you see answers are all bacteria (i.e., HHV8 not listed):
rapidFireQAs.a: Bartonella henselae; Dx is bacillary angiomatosis; bacterium causes cat scratch disease but is also known to cause Kaposi-sarcoma like lesions in immunocompromised patients.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7F + has pet cat + papules on hand + lymph node biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation + organism can be visualized using silver stain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cat scratch disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + went to pool party a week ago + has lesions on trunk as shown in image below; what’s the most likely causal organism?”
rapidFireQAs.a: poxvirus (molloscum contagiosum); largest DNA virus; classically skin-colored or reddish papules with central umbilication. Classically acquired from fomites (inanimate objects like metal railings of a pool).

rapidFireQAs.q: 9M + comes to your clinic in Brazil + black ulcer on arm + vision loss + patient is successfully treated with ivermectin; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus); nematode (roundworm helminth) transmitted by black fly; second most common cause of blindness worldwide after trachoma (Chlamydia A-C).

rapidFireQAs.q: 9M + lives in South America + swollen eyebrow + shortness of breath on exertion + S3 heart sound on examination; what’s the most likely organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: Trypanasoma cruzi (Chagas disease); protozoan; unicellular eukaryote; spread by Reduviid bug (“kissing bug” because bite is painless); can cause dilated cardiomyopathy and achalasia; swollen eyebrow is referred to as Romaña sign.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + traveled to Middle East for one month + has lesion on hand as shown below + elevated liver enzymes + pancytopenia; the organism is transmitted by sandfly; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: leishmaniasis; Leishmania donovani; protozoan; unicellular eukaryote; can cause visceral disease known as kala azar, which is associated with ↑ LFTs and pancytopenia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + works at aquarium + presents with lesions as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mycobacterium marinum; causes red ulcers/blisters on hand/arm of those who are exposed to aquatics. Do not choose Staph aureus if they specifically say aquarium / waterpark in the question.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + received renal transplant last year + has preauricular reddish lesion shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer on USMLE = Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI); can cause lymphadenitis with classic reddish/violaceous lesion on the neck or preauricularly; MAI classically causes lung disease in older women (Lady Windermere syndrome) and AIDS patients.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + recently immigrated to US from Libya with adult children + hypoesthesia of hands to pain and temperature + nodularity of fingers and nose; the most likely causal organism most likely bears what characteristic?
rapidFireQAs.a: “temperature sensitivity”; Dx = leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae); grows at cooler temperatures, so can affect the peripheral nerves and nose → can cause neuropathy and disfiguration of face (leonine facies) and limbs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + Hx of Celiac disease + lesions on elbows as shown in below photo; what is most likely to be seen on skin biopsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: IgA deposition at dermal papillae; diagnosis is dermatitis herpetiformis (not actual herpes, in contrast to eczema herpeticum; don’t confuse these conditions); this is a cutaneous eruption that can occur in patients with Celiac.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35M + Hx of ulcerative colitis + lesion on forearm as shown in below photo; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: pyoderma gangrenosum; described as ulcer with necrotic debris; rare cutaneous manifestation in IBD (usually ulcerative colitis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + African-American + high serum calcium + image shown + biopsy of lung tissue shows non- caseating granulomas; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Image is erythema nodosum. Patient has sarcoidosis. Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat); can be caused by autoimmune diseases like sarcoidosis and Crohn, as well as part of serum sickness due to medications (e.g., sulfa).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + episodes of bloody stool over past two years + perianal abscesses/fistulae seen on physical examination; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Crohn disease; increased risk since transmural inflammation in Crohn.

rapidFireQAs.q: 46M + pain during defecation + perianal skin tag visualized on physical exam + patient won’t allow rectal exam due to exquisite pain; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: anal fissure; usually posterior in the midline; NBME answer is Sitz bath for treatment.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M + painful 2-cm mass located at superior aspect of gluteal cleft; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pilonidal cyst/abscess; Tx = surgical closure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + receives IM ceftriaxone + oral azithromycin for pelvic inflammatory disease; 3-5 days later she has red rash in area of injection; diagnosis? → answer = Arthus reaction; type III hypersensitivity; can be distinguished from type I (immediate) because type III takes a few days to appear.
rapidFireQAs.a: 20F + receives IM ceftriaxone + gets polyarthritis a few days later; Dx? → answer = serum sickness; type III hypersensitivity. Arthus reaction = redness at injection site 3-5 days later. Serum sickness = polyarthritis 3-5 days after injection, drug, or acute infection. Both are type III hypersensitivites.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F with image shown below; Q asks which other condition is most immunologically similar:
rapidFireQAs.a: Image shows malar rash of SLE; answer = serum sickness, Arthus reaction, or PSGN; all four presentations are type III hypersensitivities (the correct answer is any type III hypersensitivity listed in Q answer choices; the point is to know malar rash is due to immune complexes, as are serum sickness, Arthus reaction, and PSGN).

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + increased serum creatine kinase + 3/5 strength of hips on physical exam; images as shown below; what type of antibodies are classically seen in this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: Anti-Jo1 antibodies; diagnosis is dermatomyositis; left image shows heliotrope rash; often described as violaceous eyelids; do not confuse with malar rash of SLE; right image shows shawl sign/rash; both dermatomyositis and polymyositis can have increased serum CK and/or proximal muscle weakness on physical examination (in contrast, polymyalgia rheumatica will have neither, and most often is just pain + stiffness). Muscle biopsy in polymyositis/dermatomyositis shows T cell infiltrate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + proximal muscle weakness + image shown below; Q asks for diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = dermatomyositis; image shows Gottron papules, which is a HY cutaneous finding; patients can also have “mechanics hands,” which are rough-surfaced / scaly-appearing hands; do not go chasing fungal infections here.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6F + fever 102 F + pain, erythema, and warmth of left knee + Hx of several episodes of joint pains past few years + Hb of 10.1 g/dL + MCV 72; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), aka juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA); HY for Peds; patients are susceptible to septic arthritis (as with this patient), but will often have Hx of several episodes of non-septic joint pain; anemia of chronic disease common; salmon pink body rash classic, but only seen in maybe one-third of NBME/CMS Qs, as per my observation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + hands shown in image below; Q asks melanocyte # and melanin production in following condition (i.e., ↑, ↓, or no change):
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ melanocyte #; ↓ melanin production; diagnosis is vitiligo; T cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes; can be associated with other autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, as well as IgA deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: 69F + lesion on zygoma as shown below; Q asks for for melanocyte # and melanin production:
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ melanocyte #; no change melanin production; diagnosis is lentigo (age spot; plural = lentigines).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + dark complexion + skin sample mixed up in lab with fair-skinned individual; Q asks melanocyte # and melanosome # in dark-skinned individual
rapidFireQAs.a: no change melanocyte #; ↑ melanosome #; melanosomes are organelles within melanocytes that produce melanin. Differences in skin pigmentation between individuals is due to more or less melanin, while melanocyte number is the same for all people.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + Hx of gastroesophageal reflux + hands shown in image below; Q asks for what condition this patient is most likely to develop:
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary hypertension (secondary to pulmonary fibrosis); diagnosis is limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome); left image shows Raynaud phenomenon, which is color change due to vascular spasm and reactive hyperemia; the right image shows sclerodactyly, which is tightening of skin of the digits. Raynaud phenomenon is not limited to scleroderma and can be seen in conditions such as SLE, hyperviscosity syndrome, or can be familial (erythromelalgia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + dysphagia + cracked corners of the mouth; image of nail shown below; Q asks for what is most likely to be seen in this patient:
rapidFireQAs.a: low MCV; Dx is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which is the triad of 1) esophageal webs (dysphagia), 2) angular cheilosis (cracked corners of mouth), and 3) iron deficiency anemia (severe cases can present with koilonychia [spoon-shaped nails] or pica [eating ice, clay, starch]).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + blood in stool + arthritis + erythematous/silvery scaling lesions on forehead, above upper lip, and on elbows; attempting to remove one of the skin lesions causes bleeding; diagnosis?
