rapidFireQAs.a: psoriasis; patient here also has IBD; HLA-B27 sometimes associated (PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis); Auspitz sign is bleeding of psoriatic scales with attempted removal; psoriatic lesions classically on extensor areas but can be on face/forehead; Munro microabscesses are collections of neutrophils in the skin in psoriasis; psoriatic arthritis in some patients shows “pencil-in-cup” deformity on hand x-ray; treat with topical calcipotriene (vitamin D derivative), topical steroid, or coal tar; if topicals not effective or patient has systemic psoriasis (arthritis), oral methotrexate or acitretin can be given; the latter is a vitamin A derivative.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8F + excoriations visible in flexor creases + occasional dry cough worse in winter; image of elbow shown below; Q asks what type of hypersensitivity is most likely responsible for this patient’s presentation:
rapidFireQAs.a: type I (immediate); diagnosis is atopy; image shows eczema (atopic dermatitis); patient has cough-variant asthma (1/3 of asthma patients only have dry cough, usually worse in the winter or with exercise); treat with oil-based emollient and topical corticosteroids; if steroids used >5-7 days continuously, thinning of the dermis may occur.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + history of eczema + area over elbow is red, inflamed, and oozing; 6-year-old sister recently had weeping papules on face; Dx in the 18-year-old?
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus or Group A Strep superinfection over eczema; likely inoculated from younger sister’s impetigo.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + recently treated with azithromycin for chlamydial urethritis; forearm is shown in below photo; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: urticaria (hives); type I hypersensitivity; can be precipitated by various allergens, including pollen, pet dander, and drugs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 39M + went hiking + used sunscreen over body + has linear vesicles on legs; Q asks best way to prevent this condition; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “avoidance of contact with weeds”; diagnosis is contact dermatitis due to poison ivy/sumac; linear vesicles is hugely HY descriptor for poison ivy/oak/sumac; sunscreen will be the answer if they say rash on dorsa of hands, arms, and face (i.e., it’s everywhere); nickel will be the answer for contact dermatitis if they mention vesicles on the wrist in someone who wears a watch; USMLE also loves latex allergy as red rash on hands of someone using gloves as anatomy proctor or working as nurse in new facility, as well as adhesives allergy (i.e., from bandages in hospital); contact dermatitis is type IV hypersensitivity (T cell-mediated); rash will appear within days of exposure to irritant + will take a few days to go away following removal of the irritant.

rapidFireQAs.q: 38F + recently treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for simple UTI + develops sloughing skin over her arms; image shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Stevens-Johnson syndrome → autoimmune type IV hypersensitivity (T cell response) resulting in detachment of skin covering <10% surface area of body; Nikolsky sign is (+), which is sloughing of the skin with friction. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is sloughing of >30% surface area; 10-30% is an intermediate form; classically caused by sulfa drugs and anti-epileptics (lamotrigine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + tattoo a couple days ago + image shown below; Q asks for Dx:
rapidFireQAs.a: contact dermatitis from tattoo ink; asked on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + nurse + allergic to bananas + image of hands shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: Latex allergy (contact dermatitis; type IV hypersensitivity); patients who are allergic to bananas are often allergic to latex; contact dermatitis secondary to medical adhesives (i.e., bandages) can also occur, causing well-demarcated rash.

rapidFireQAs.q: 38F + chronic dry skin on the legs + scratches same area repeatedly; no other past medical history; image shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lichen simplex chronicus; dry, excoriated skin due to repeated scratching; dry, excoriated skin due to repeated scratching. The word excoriated means scratched. It's an important vocab word for Derm.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23M + painful vesicular lesions on the lip + fever + lymphadenopathy + presents with rash on arms as shown in below photo; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Erythema multiforme; immune complex-mediated rash (type III hypersensitivity) with many etiologies; HSV1/2 is classic cause; can also be caused by drugs (e.g., sulfa).

rapidFireQAs.q: 21M + blistering skin lesions + oral involvement + no mention of medications recently taken + Nikolsky sign (+); Q asks for the molecular target of the antibodies seen in this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: desmosomes (desmoglein proteins), which mediate adjacent keratinocyte adhesion; diagnosis is pemphigus vulgaris, which is a blistering autoimmune skin condition caused by antibodies against desmosomes; oral involvement is common; Nikolsky sign is positive; immunofluorescence will show a net-like pattern.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21M + blistering skin lesions + no oral involvement + no mention of medications recently taken + Nikolsky sign negative; Q asks for the molecular target of the antibodies seen in this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemidesmosomes, which stabilize basal epithelial cells to the basement membrane; diagnosis is bullous pemphigoid; less severe than pemphigus vulgaris; usually no oral involvement; Nikolsky is negative; immunofluorescence shows a linear pattern.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21M + formation of skin blisters with minor trauma; Q asks for what type of cell-cell interaction is disrupted in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: “basal:suprabasal” → Weird answer, but on NBME they write it just like that with the colon separating the words; diagnosis is epidermolysis bullosa, which is due to mutations (not antibodies, as with the aforementioned PV and BP) in keratin 5 and 14 of the dermal- epidermal junction; formation of blisters with trauma is not Nikolsky sign; the latter is removal / sloughing of the skin with friction, not blister formation with friction.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26M + oral + genital ulcers + high ESR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Behcet disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 63M + patchy facial erythema that worsens with spicy foods and alcohol; slight pain of rash in cold weather; image of patient is below; Q asks simply for diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: rosacea; multifactorial etiology; described as mix of itchy and painful facial rash in middle age patient that gets worse with things like cold weather, alcohol, and spicy food; topical metronidazole sometimes effective, as with avoidance of certain triggers like spicy food or alcohol. Rhinophyma is a severe bulbous enlargement of the nose that can occur in some patients with rosacea.

rapidFireQAs.q: 46M + high serum calcium + CXR shows bilar lymphadenopathy + image of face is shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lupus pernio (a cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis, not SLE, despite the name).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + presents during winter + painful/itchy toes + topical antifungals not effective; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: perniosis (chilblains); painful inflammation of distal capillaries due to repeated exposure to cold air, followed by immersion in hot water (i.e., from bath/shower). This is different from frostnip and frostbite. Frostnip is cold-exposed skin (effects quickly reversible; no skin damage); frostbite is more severe and can result in damage such as blistering and necrosis. Can sometimes be intensely itchy and hence confused with tinea pedis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + occasional painful single mouth ulcers (image shown below); Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = aphthous ulcers (aphthous stomatitis); no Tx necessary; not related to HSV1/2; etiology is multifactorial; can be precipitated by allergens such as spice; T cell-mediated.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + mouth ulcers + fever + treated two days ago for hyperthyroidism in hospital; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Drug-induced neutropenia. Propylthiouracil and methimazole are thionamides (anti-thyroid drugs) that can both cause neutropenia (aka agranulocytosis), which can present as mouth ulcers (mucositis). Propylthiouracil is one of the drugs that is classically used for thyroid storm, so a recent hospitalization for hyperthyroidism suggests the patient was probably given this drug and now has neutropenia. HY drugs for neutropenia are the thionamides, clozapine, methotrexate, and TMP/SMX.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37M + occasional itchy bumps on hands; sometimes in ring-like pattern; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = granuloma annulare; caused by cutaneous T cell response; occurs in young, healthy patients; may present as small bumps that progress to annular/ring-like pattern; self- resolving + no Tx necessary.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + hepatitis C positive + purple, pruritic skin lesions; image shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lichen planus; classically described as “The Ps” → purple, pruritic, polygonal papules; however Qs need not mention they’re pruritic; hepatitis C + red/purple skin lesions = lichen planus. I've also seen it occur idiopathically on NBME. USMLE wants you to know this often just self-resolves if no treatment is initiated.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + thrombocytopenia + polyarthritis + chronic sores of the cheeks and scalp + anti-Smith antibody positive; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE; dermatologic component is discoid lupus, which is a severe cutaneous presentation seen sometimes in SLE patients, with sores/scarring of the face, scalp, and ears; thrombocytopenia (and leuko-/erythropenia) is seen in many SLE patients due to anti- hematologic cell line antibodies; arthritis is the most common presenting feature in SLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born to mother who took methimazole during first trimester; photo of child is shown; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: aplasia cutis congenita; absence of skin on an area of scalp; can be caused by teratogens such as methimazole.

rapidFireQAs.q: 5M + second episode of edema of face, hands, and arms; patient is prescribed danazol; image of patient is shown below; what is the most likely mechanism for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (not C1 esterase alone); diagnosis is hereditary angioedema; condition characterized by recurrent swelling of various bodily regions; danazol (androgen receptor partial agonist) causes liver to produce more C1 esterase inhibitor.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + third trimester of pregnancy + itchy rash around umbilicus + stretch marks not involved; image is shown below; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is gestational pemphigoid; does not involve stretchmarks (unlike PUPPP); cause is sporadic/multifactorial; Tx is oral or topical steroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + third trimester of pregnancy + intense, diffuse pruritis, especially on palms + soles; no skin rash; serum bile acids are elevated; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; Dx by measuring increased serum bile acids; Tx is ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol).

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + nosebleeds for the past week + petechial rash + bleeding time 9 minutes + platelet count 90,000/uL; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: idiopathic (immune) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); cause is antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa on platelets (type II HS); Dx with decreased platelet count (answer on NBME; increased bleeding time for Dx is wrong answer). Tx = steroids first, then IVIG, then splenectomy is definitive.

rapidFireQAs.q: 67M + lesion shown on nose in photo below; Q simply asks the diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: basal cell carcinoma (BCC); on USMLE, classically pearlescent / slightly translucent; talengiectasias common; can be described as having “heaped up borders” or “rolled edges”; may or may not be ulcerated. Treatment for skin cancers on cosmetically sensitive areas such as the eyelid or nose can be managed with Mohs micrographic surgery (on NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + atypical skin lesion on neck + biopsy shows clusters of basophilic cells (shown below); Q asks for the diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: BCC; histo shows clusters of basophilic (purple) cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M + receives topical immunomodulator for confirmed BCC; what is the drug he received?
rapidFireQAs.a: imiquimod; stimulates toll-like receptor-7 (TLR-7).

rapidFireQAs.q: 62F + farmer + lesions on forearm/hand shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: actinic keratoses (aka solar keratoses); precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); classically described as red/scaly lesions on forehead, ear, or arms of fisherman, farmers, or construction workers. Can also appear as rough whiteish lesions on the hands/forearms. Cryotherapy is an answer for treatment on NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: 74M + fisherman; forehead and ear are shown below; Q asks for the diagnosis of the ear lesion:
rapidFireQAs.a: Forehead shows actinic keratoses. Ear shows squamous cell carcinoma; actinic keratoses can classically progress to SCC; patient has many actinic keratoses and was likely at risk of developing SCC, as with the ear lesion; on USMLE, SCC will not have telangiectasias or pearlescent/translucent appearance (as with BCC). Both SCC and BCC can be ulcerated and/or have rolled edges (I’ve seen rolled/ulcerated SCC on NBME exam, even though rolled edges are textbook BCC. But with that particular Q the patient had actinic keratoses, so you know SCC is what progresses from that). Do not memorize BCC vs SCC as necessarily occurring in certain locations (i.e., upper vs lower lip, etc.). USMLE has zero regard for this stuff. You need to look for telangiectasias and pearly appearance for BCC, versus absence for SCC.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60M + 2 packs cigarettes daily for 30 years + lesion on back; biopsy is shown below; Q asks Dx:
rapidFireQAs.a: SCC; histo shows keratin pearls (pink circles), which are classic for SCC; USMLE wants you to know “keratin pearls + intercellular bridges” = SCC. Smoking + immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV) are HY risk factors for SCC.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F + rough-surfaced grey/white lesion on labia majora; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lichen sclerosus; described as rough, white/grey, patchy, and/or itchy area on vulva or perineum; must do biopsy to rule out SCC before topical steroids; the latter are effective treatment. If the Q gives an overtly ulcerated lesion on the vulva in this demographic, the diagnosis is vulvar carcinoma, where lichen sclerosus is the wrong answer. LS will not be described as ulcerated.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + lesion on face shown below; Q asks for the diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: keratoacanthoma; can be confused with SCC; described as fast-growing and dome- shaped with a hyperkeratotic core, surrounded by a wall of inflamed skin; can sometimes self-regress, but Tx is still surgical excision.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + confirmed melanoma + receives aldesleukin; Q asks which cytokine this relates to?
rapidFireQAs.a: IL-2; aldesleukin is a recombinant interleukin-2 that can be used in the treatment of melanoma and RCC; IL-2 normally functions to stimulate T cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + African-American + lesion on foot as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: acral lentiginous melanoma; melanoma of palms/soles (areas not usually exposed to sun); more common in persons of African and Asian descent.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + Asian-American + fingernail shown in photo below; diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: acral lentiginous melanoma; USMLE will show you image of ALM on the palm/sole, or it can be subungual (as shown here).

rapidFireQAs.q: 29M + nailbed lesion + radiating pain incited by cold temperature; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: glomus tumor; The glomus body is a type of modified smooth muscle cell in fingers/toes that assists in thermoregulation. Sounds arcane/weird, but for some magical reason exists on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 67M + lesion on face as shown in photo below; biopsy shows malignant cells growing laterally along the basement membrane without dermal invasion; Q asks diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: lentigo maligña; considered melanoma in situ; starts as black/brown “stain” that grows laterally within stratum basale without penetration; once it invades, it is called lentigo maligña melanoma (Hutchinson melanotic freckle); the terminology can sound confusing because lentigo maligña is still technically melanoma, albeit in situ, but once it invades it takes on “melanoma” as the suffix. This is on NBME exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + confirmed melanoma + two other first-degree family members also had melanoma; Q asks for which gene is most likely associated in this patient
rapidFireQAs.a: BRAF; proto-oncogene, not a tumor suppressor; BRAF codes for BRAF serine-threonine kinase. You do not need to know vemurafenib (targets BRAF kinase) for USMLE, but some students have asked about it.

rapidFireQAs.q: 83F + facial lesions shown in photo below; Q asks for diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: seborrheic keratoses; sun exposure and old age are biggest risk factors; described as “greasy,” or waxy, skin growths that appear like they can be “peeled off”; not malignant. Sign of Leser-Trélat = sudden, eruptive seborrheic keratoses secondary to underlying, visceral malignancy (i.e., unrelated to age or sun).

rapidFireQAs.q: 15M + mouth shown in photo below; Q asks for what kind of polyps he most likely has:
rapidFireQAs.a: hamartomatous; Dx is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; combination of perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) and hamartomatous colonic polyps. Perioral melanosis also seen in Carney complex (cardiac myxoma in a kid, perioral melanosis, endocrine hypersecretion). Not with you. It’s on the USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + jaw lesion as shown in photo below; Q asks for molecular function of gene involved:
rapidFireQAs.a: transcription factor; Dx is Burkitt lymphoma; usually t(8;14) translocation; c-MYC gene; codes for transcription factor; “starry sky” appearance on histo. Focus here isn’t heme/onc, but HY contrasting point: do not confuse with follicular lymphoma, which is t(14;18) translocation, BCL-2 gene; codes for anti-apoptotic molecule; presents as waxing/waning neck mass over 1-2 years.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + smoker + rough, white lesion on lateral aspect of tongue that does not scrape off; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: leukoplakia; precancerous lesion to SCC; caused by smoking / chewing tobacco.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + HIV positive + white lesions on lateral tongue that do not scrape off; Q asks for the viral etiology
rapidFireQAs.a: EBV; Dx is oral hairy leukoplakia; not precancerous; caused by hyperkeratosis (excessive skin proliferation); one of the most common presentations of HIV (in addition to oropharyngeal candidiasis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + IV drug-user + lesion on leg shown in photo below + biopsy shows malignant T cells with cerebriform nuclei; Q asks which virus is most likely responsible:
rapidFireQAs.a: Human T cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV-1/2); diagnosis is mycosis fungoides, which is a cutaneous T cell lymphoma; T cells have nuclei with classic “cerebriform” appearance; Pautrier microabscesses are atypical T cells in epidermis; HTLV-1/2 is retrovirus (RNA, enveloped) most similar to HIV; increased prevalence in IV drug-users and persons in Japan and Caribbean; you do not need to be able to do a spot-diagnosis here; Q will pretty much always give you enough descriptors in the vignette.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + Hx of IV drug-use + diffuse red body rash as shown in photo below + blood smear shows leukemic T cells with cerebriform nuclei; Q asks for structure of viral etiology (i.e., RNA vs DNA; enveloped vs non-enveloped):
rapidFireQAs.a: RNA, enveloped; virus is HTLV-1/2; diagnosis is Sezary syndrome; T cell leukemic extension of mycosis fungoides; diffuse exfoliative erythroderma is classic.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + had gallbladder removed at age 58 + afebrile + abdomen shown below; Q asks next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: CT of abdomen with contrast; Dx is pancreatic cancer; image shows jaundice (yes, I jacked up the saturation to make the patient yellow AF); remote cholecystectomy denotes impossibility of choledocholithiasis; this Q asked on Surg NBME; if the Q tells you in the last line that CT shows no abnormalities, next best step = ERCP to look for cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer). Head of pancreas cancer impinges on common bile duct → jaundice with increased ALP and direct bilirubin; pancreatic enzymes are normal; if gallstone pancreatitis, enzymes up.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + history of shooting groin pain + elevated serum glucose + red rash on abdomen; Q asks for which pancreatic cancer type is the Dx
rapidFireQAs.a: glucagonoma → can cause ↑ glucose + necrolytic migratory erythema (rash). Patient has MEN1 (pancreas, parathyroid, pituitary); shooting groin pain = ureterolithiasis; hyperparathyroidism → high Ca2+ → stones.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + flushing of face + diarrhea + low serum potassium; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: VIPoma; classically WDHA syndrome → Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, Achlorhydria; can also cause facial flushing.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + 20 weeks’ gestation + scattered skin lesions on trunk and arms, as shown in photo below; patient also has axillary/groin freckling; Q asks inheritance pattern:
rapidFireQAs.a: autosomal dominant; Dx is neurofibromatosis type I (NF1); image shows café au lait spot; one of the phakomatoses (neurocutaneous disorders → NF1/2, VHL, TSC, Sturge- Weber); NF1 → café au lait spots, neurofibromas, axillary/groin freckling, optic glioma, pheochromocytoma; for some reason, USMLE likes NF1 in obgyn Qs, even though the condition is genetic / unrelated to obgyn.

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + lesions shown on face in image below; Q asks inheritance pattern:
rapidFireQAs.a: autosomal dominant; Dx is tuberous sclerosis (TSC); image shows adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas); one of the phakomatoses; in TSC we see intracranial / periventricular nodules (tubers, aka cortical hamartomas), adenoma sebaceum, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangeoleiomyomatosis, subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, Ashleaf spots, and Shagreen patches.

rapidFireQAs.q: 17M + Hx of epilepsy + physical examination shows violaceous papules in a temporal distribution; Dx? → answer = Sturge-Weber; classically Port Wine-stain birthmark (nevus flammeus) in textbooks, but USMLE can describe this as “violaceous papules in a temporal distribution”; associated with leptomeningeal angioma (causing seizure) and glaucoma.
rapidFireQAs.a: Classic Port wine stain birthmark, as seen in Sturge-Weber; condition is not inherited and is due to somatic mosaicism.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + deficiency of a-galactosidase A + buildup of ceramide trihexoside + heart/kidney issues + red lesions on skin shown in image below; Q asks diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: Fabry disease; lysosomal storage disease; X-linked recessive; image shows angiokeratomas, which are dilated capillaries forming papules.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + skin lesions as shown in image below + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + testes large for gestational age; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: McCune-Albright syndrome → triad of “coast of Maine” café au lait spots (above image), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (bone is replaced by fibrous tissue), and endocrine hypersecretion (classically precocious puberty).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + retained primary teeth + eczema + recurrent Staphylococcal abscesses; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hyper- IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) → FATED → coarse Facies, Staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, hyper-IgE, Dermatologic abnormalities (eczema).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + delayed separation of umbilical cord at birth + recurrent skin infections without pus + biopsy shows decreased neutrophils at sites of skin infection; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: leukocyte adhesion deficiency; defective LFA-1/CD18 integrin.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonatal male + family recently immigrated to US from China; back is shown in image below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Diagnosis is Mongolian spot (blue nevus), a form of benign birthmark where dermal melanocytes fail to migrate superficially to stratum basale. Often mistaken for child abuse. Schedule routine follow-up. Wrong answer is contacting child protective services.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + BMI 36 + neck shown in image below; what is most likely to be seen in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperinsulinemia; image is acanthosis nigricans (brown/black velvety skin, usually along nape of neck); associated with hyperinsulinemia and type II diabetes; can also rarely be seen in patients with underlying, visceral malignancy (e.g., gastric adenocarcinoma).

rapidFireQAs.q: 42M + lantern jaw + increased hat/shoe size + high BP + image shown below; Q asks next best step in diagnosis:
rapidFireQAs.a: measure serum insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-1); wrong answer is measure serum growth hormone; diagnosis is acromegaly; GH causes liver to secrete IGF-1, which in turn promotes growth of tissues; skin tags can be seen secondary to insulin resistance; growth hormone excess causes insulin resistance (tangential, but for Step 1, choose ↑ activity for catabolic/gluconeogenic enzymes; ↓ activity for anabolic enzymes, since ↓ insulin effect).

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + coloboma of the iris + ventricular septal defect + ear is shown below; Q asks what else is likely to be seen in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: atresia of the choanae; Dx is CHARGE syndrome → Coloboma of the iris, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae (baby turns blue during breastfeeding and pink when crying; Dx by inserting nasogastric tube), Retardation of growth/development, Genitourinary anomalies, Ear anomalies (protruding ears with lack of earlobe).

rapidFireQAs.q: 7M + hole seen on preauricular aspect of ear bilaterally; patient is asymptomatic; Q asks treatment:
rapidFireQAs.a: no Tx necessary; preauricular pits are benign finding, usually not associated with any congenital disorder; can become infected; surgical closure if frequent infections.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + lesion superior to pinna in image shown below; Dx+ Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx is strawberry hemangioma; benign capillary tumor in neonates that will grow slightly then regress spontaneously within a few years; no Tx necessary unless causing functional impairment.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + photo of lesions on neck shown below; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cherry hemangiomas; no Tx necessary; benign capillary tumors caused by UV light; greater prevalence with increasing age. Students confuse with strawberry hemangioma in peds.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + tuft of hair seen on lower back; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: spina bifida occulta; NBME exam has one answer written as “spinal dysraphism,” rather than spina bifida.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + long-standing Hx of ulcerative colitis managed with multiple medications; abdomen shown in image below. What is causing this skin presentation:
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing syndrome due to exogenous prednisone used in autoimmune disease; USMLE wants you to know purple striae are classically Cushing. This is due to weakening of dermal collagen and capillary walls, with micro bleeding into skin. Cushing syndrome can also cause hyperpigmentation due to ↑ ACTH in some patients, including patients with small cell who have ectopic ACTH secretion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 41M + serum glucose 130 mg/dL + sore hands + hand x-ray shows Heberden nodes; physical exam shows darkening of the skin of the forearms; Q asks next best step in diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum ferritin; Dx is hereditary hemochromatosis; can present as “bronze diabetes” → diabetes due to deposition of iron in tail of pancreas; hemosiderin deposition in skin causes hyperpigmentation (hemosiderosis); arthritis is pseudogout, not osteoarthritis (two of the biggest risk factors for pseudogout are hereditary hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism; can present as OA- like presentation in someone with aforementioned conditions, or as monoarthritis of large joint, such as the knee).

rapidFireQAs.q: 30M + 6-month-Hx of fatigue + serum potassium 6.0 mEq/L, sodium 130 mEq/L, bicarb 20 mEq/L + eosinophils 23% + hyperpigmentation of forearms; Q asks which diagnostic test should be performed?
rapidFireQAs.a: ACTH stimulation test; Dx is Addison disease (primary hypoadrenalism); classically low sodium, high potassium, and low bicarb when aldosterone is low; low cortisol can cause eosinophilia; do not go chasing stool ova and parasites; hyperpigmentation in the setting of low cortisol is due to decreased negative feedback at the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary → increased POMC, which is the precursor to both ACTH and a-MSH; both ACTH and a-MSH can increase pigmentation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + brought in by mother for pain in right arm after falling off swing on playground; x-ray shows fracture of the humerus; photo of hand shown below; Q asks next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: contact child protect services; photo shows classic circular appearance of cigarette burn; can also be on face / resemble impetigo if at different stages of healing; humerus fractures uncommon and can be from blunt-force trauma; child abuse classically spiral fractures (rotational force), but emphasis in above Q is the cigarette burn.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + lesions on ear shown in image below + occurred following removal of ear piercings several weeks ago; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: keloid scars; disorganized growth of collagen type I and III; scar grows beyond boundaries of original wound; In contrast, hypertrophic scars may resemble keloids but do not grow beyond boundaries of original wound; Tx is surgical excision, although recurrence is common. Benign.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + face shown in photo below; vitals normal; no past medical Hx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps); increased prevalence in African descent; curly beard hair grows back into the skin; Tx is to allow the beard to grow; USMLE Q will show you image and just ask the spot-Dx.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + Hx of pain in buttocks/thighs when walking his dog + image of foot shown; what’s the most likely cause of this finding?
rapidFireQAs.a: arterial insufficiency; image shows arterial ulcer; often punched-out in appearance, well-demarcated; usually tops/bottoms of feet/toes; patients will frequently have Hx of intermittent claudication, diabetes, CABG, etc. Peripheral pulses will be decreased (i.e., popliteal and dorsalis pedis). Arterial disease is often associated with trophic changes of legs demonstrating shiny skin with loss of hair.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + image shown below; what’s the most likely cause of this finding?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic venous insufficiency; image shows venous ulcer; classically large, sloughy lesion around the ankle / medial malleolus; hyperpigmentation common in venous disease due to congestion and hemosiderin extravasation (“brawny edema”). Peripheral pulses are normal in venous disease. USMLE wants you to be able to spot-diagnose arterial vs venous ulcers.

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + leg shown below; no other past medical Hx; Q asks for next best step in Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Image shows varicose veins; Dx → Duplex venous ultrasonography for venous disease / valvular insufficiency; Tx is compression stockings; do not choose surgical interventions for varicose veins on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + 1-cm painful, palpable “cord” around the ankle / tracks up toward the knee; image is shown below; Q asks for Tx:
rapidFireQAs.a: Answer on NBME = subcutaneous enoxaparin; Dx is superficial thrombophlebitis; similar to DVT, but in more superficial vein; treated with heparin; wrong answer is compression stockings; difficult Q since compression stockings common answer for venous disease, but if patient has active venous occlusion (i.e., DVT or superficial thrombophlebitis), give heparin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 48M + heavy smoker + hands shown below + no other significant past medical history; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); Tx = smoking cessation; presents as digital gangrene in males who are heavy smokers.

rapidFireQAs.q: 66F + type II diabetes + HbA1c 9.8% + metoclopramide is one of her meds; image of foot shown below; x-ray of the foot shows disorganization of the tarsals/metatarsals; Q asks most likely cause of the lesion shown:
rapidFireQAs.a: “lack of appropriate joint sensation”; Dx = Charcot joint (neuropathic joint); patient cannot feel her feet due to peripheral neuropathy; vignette description points away from pure arterial ulcer (plus arterial ulcers are more distal/punched-out, rather than around the ankle); metoclopramide implies patient has diabetic gastroparesis, hence is on the prokinetic; gastroparesis implies advanced neuropathy; USMLE can give you Hx of neurogenic/hypotonic bladder as well (i.e., on bethanechol).

rapidFireQAs.q: 62M + hepatitis C + decreased serum C4 + legs shown in image below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cryoglobulinemia (presenting as livedo reticularis) secondary to hepatitis C; cryoglobulins are immune complexes that precipitate at cold temperatures (type III HS); livedo reticularis is a mottled, reticulated vascular pattern that has many etiologies; cryoglobulinemia is associated with decreased serum complement protein C4 (in contrast, C3 is sometimes down in SLE flares and Group A Strep infections).

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + smoker + appearance shown in photos below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Pancoast tumor causing SVC syndrome; photos show Pemberton sign (facial erythema/plethora due to diminished venous return when arms are raised above head). Children with ALL who have (+) Pemberton sign have T cell variant (thymic lesion); normally ALL is B cell, without thymic lesion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + alcoholism + image shown below; Q asks which vessel(s) is/are experiencing congestion:
rapidFireQAs.a: superficial epigastric veins; Dx is caput medusae; sometimes seen in severe portal hypertension secondary to cirrhosis. Don't confuse with "left gastric vein," which is often the answer for esophageal varices (i.e., portal → left gastric → esophageal veins).

rapidFireQAs.q: 70F + chronic alcoholism + hands shown below; Q asks mechanism for this finding:
rapidFireQAs.a: “failure of the liver to degrade estrogen”; palmar erythema (above image), spider angiomata, and gynecomastia are classic hyper-estrogenic findings seen in advanced liver disease; Q can also have “hyperestrogenism” as the answer; if the latter isn’t listed, “decreased testosterone” is also correct on one of the NBMEs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70M + smoker + recently underwent AAA repair + foot shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cholesterol emboli; due to embolization of cholesterol plaques to distal vasculature; Hx of AAA repair classic; atheromata launch off to distal arterioles/capillaries.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + snowboarding accident where he collided with tree + severely painful and distorted left thigh + platelets are 50,000/uL; on examination, patient’s chest is shown below; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fat embolism; patient has femoral shaft fracture → release of bone marrow fat into blood → chelates platelets → thrombocytopenia; petechial rash on chest due to occlusion of microvasculature by fat; thrombocytopenia in and of itself is not responsible for petechial rash (for instance, this finding is not classic in ITP).

rapidFireQAs.q: 49M + rash over axillae + alopecia + diminished smell and taste; Q asks which nutrient is deficient
rapidFireQAs.a: zinc; classically causes anosmia (decreased smell) + hypogeusia (decreased taste), but the vignette need not mention these findings. Can also cause alopecia and rash. Neonates with congenital malabsorption (acrodermatitis enteropathica) can have rash on face.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + “appears ill” + bruises on forearms + bleeding around hair follicles and from gums; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: scurvy (vitamin C deficiency); perifollicular hemorrhages and oral mucosal bleeding are classic.

rapidFireQAs.q: 70M + image of neck shown below; Q asks for nutrient deficiency:
rapidFireQAs.a: niacin (vitamin B3); image shows Casal necklace; B3 deficiency causes pellagra → 3Ds → dementia, dermatitis, diarrhea; the photodermatitis is classically Casal necklace, but can also be described as merely hyperpigmentation of the forearms in a patient with increased bowel motions and delirium (one of the biggest risk factors for delirium is underlying dementia).

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + drinks plenty of alcohol and bags of nucleic acids; image of painful toe is shown below; Tx? -
rapidFireQAs.a: indomethacin (NSAID), colchicine (microtubule inhibitor), or prednisone; diagnosis is acute gout; chronic gout managed first-line with xanthine oxidase inhibitor (i.e., allopurinol or febuxostat) between attacks. “What are the layers of the skin?” You might say, “Yo that’s weird you didn’t mention this first thing cuz it’s hyper-basic.” → Reason I held off is because USMLE doesn’t directly assess, “What are the skin layers?” But it would be odd not mentioning them at all since this is literally a dermatology PDF.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + long time spent in sun + erythema over 70% of her body; Dx + Tx? → answer = first-degree burn (sunburn); Tx = supportive care / no Tx necessary; do not select answers such as silver sulfadiazine, etc.
rapidFireQAs.a: First-degree (superficial) burn → epidermis only → diffuse erythema + pain. Second-degree (superficial partial) → involves papillary dermis → blistering + pain. Second-degree (deep partial) → involves reticular dermis → white/leathery; painless. Third-degree (deep; full-thickness) → involves hypodermis → painless. Fourth-degree → involves underlying muscle, tendon, or bone. I have not seen silver sulfadiazine and triple antibiotic ointment as answers on NBME assessments; literature is mixed on their use.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about dumb molecular skin stuff? Like the connective proteins and stuff.”
rapidFireQAs.a: Tight junction is the answer if they ask what prevents movement of solute between cells (i.e., prevents water from getting through your skin). They can also ask about this in relation to gastrointestinal mucosa (i.e., person with IBD demonstrates radiolabeled substance in blood after it was injected into bowel; however person without IBD does not have the substance in the blood; why? → answer = loss of tight junction function in IBD patient. Tight junctions contain proteins called claudins and occludins. Adherens junction is the answer if they ask about what connects the actin cytoskeleton of adjacent cells. E-cadherins are essential proteins (E-cadherins compose adherens junctions); E-cadherins are calcium-dependent. Desmosome is the answer for pemphigus vulgaris and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; composed to desmoglein proteins. Gap junctions contain connexin proteins. Unrelated to skin, but I’ve seen this asked for myocardial muscle electrical conduction (i.e., how is electrical synchrony accomplished?) → answer = gap junctions. I’ve seen “connexin” as distractor answer on NBME, but never as correct answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE Q asks which layer vitamin D synthesis starts in → answer = stratum basale.
rapidFireQAs.a: 7-dehydrocholesterol in stratum basale, via UV-B radiation, → cholecalciferol. § NBME Q tells you patient does not get sunlight and asks “synthesis of which substrate is impaired?” → answer = cholecalciferol; 7-dehydrocholesterol is wrong answer. Cholecalciferol goes to liver and takes on 25-hydroxylation, becoming 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol). § If patient has liver disease, 25-OH-D3 is ↓; answer can also be “decreased hepatic hydroxylation.” 25-OH-D3 goes to the kidney and takes on the 1-hydroxylation, via 1a-hydroxylase, under the action of parathyroid hormone → 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol). 1,25-(OH)2-D3 then goes to the small bowel and increases absorption of Ca2+ and PO43-; it also goes to bone and converts unmineralized osteoid → mineralized hydroxyapatite. - “Do I need to know stuff like macule, patch, plaque, etc.? Various terminology?” → Yes, but this stuff more just applies to terms thrown around in USMLE vignettes. In other words, you will not get asked directly, “Is this a patch?” Or, “Is this a vesicle vs bulla?” Etc. Macule: flat lesion <1cm. Patch: flat lesion >1cm; classically café au lait spots in NF1. Papule: raised lesion <1cm; “maculopapular” → many viral rashes and drug reactions. Plaque: raised lesion >1cm; psoriasis. Vesicle: clear-fluid collection <5mm; HSV1/2, or shingles (VZV). Bulla: clear-fluid collection >5mm; bullous impetigo (S. aureus); pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, epidermolysis bullosa.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + brought in by ambulance following motorcycle accident + BP 160/100 + HR 52 + respiratory rate 10; image of patient shown below; Q asks mechanism for patient’s hypertension:
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased intracranial pressure”; image shows Battle sign (bruising over mastoid process seen in base of skull fracture); patient can also have racoon eyes, rhinorrhea, and otorrhea in base of skull fracture; Cushing reflex = hypertension, bradycardia, and bradypnea as a result of increased intracranial pressure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + 2nd degree burn on leg from playing with fireworks + heals; 3 months later, area of burn appears darker than surrounding skin; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; benign hyperpigmentation that can occur following inflammation (as the name implies); no Tx necessary; usually self-resolving; if topicals used, hydroquinone or tretinoin often effective.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + on combined oral contraceptive pills for 12 years + slightly hyperpigmented skin on cheeks and buttocks; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: melasma (chloasma); benign hyperpigmentation of skin usually due to estrogen-containing OCPs or pregnancy; worsened with sun exposure; no Tx necessary; can consider stopping OCPs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + alcoholic + brought in from the snow in the winter; student Q showed pic of dude’s red feet following rewarming and they asked what electrolyte (high or low) we’re most worried about
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperkalemia → alcoholics susceptible to rhabdomyolysis → lysis of cells releases potassium + myoglobin is nephrotoxic and can cause acute tubular necrosis and hyperkalemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 74-year-old man living in Las Vegas + smoker + no other past medical Hx + they show you following image; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: actinic purpura (aka senile or solar purpura). These are flat, purple discolorations caused by damage to dermal collagen and blood vessels due to chronic sun exposure. Commonly appear on the back of the hands and forearms in elderly. Benign; may be mistaken for bruises. NBME Q describes actinic purpura and then asks for mechanism. The answer is “solar elastosis,” which is a term that refers to degenerative changes to the dermis due to chronic sun exposure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 14F + no past medical history + has irritation on her arms that she finds embarrassing + Q shows you following image; Q asks diagnosis straight-up. -
rapidFireQAs.a: Diagnosis = keratosis pilaris. Benign bumps + rough patches on the skin due to build-up of excess keratin. The excess Keratin can block hair follicles and pores, causing small, hard bumps. No treatment necessary. Emollients may be used. Not obscure condition I’m mentioning for fun. Shows up on NBME. “Do I need to know the nerve endings in skin and stuff like that?” Annoyingly, they do show up: Cutaneous nerve endings + what they detect

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for tinea capitis
rapidFireQAs.a: oral griseofulvin for patient only

rapidFireQAs.q: How to decrease risk of tinea capitis
rapidFireQAs.a: avoidance of sharing of hats

rapidFireQAs.q: Hypopigmentation on upper back / trunk
rapidFireQAs.a: tinea versicolor (Malassezia furfur)

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of impetigo
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus now exceeds S. pyogenes

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of impetigo
rapidFireQAs.a: topical mupirocin

rapidFireQAs.q: Beefy red, well-demarcated skin plaque
rapidFireQAs.a: erysipelas

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of erysipelas
rapidFireQAs.a: Group A Strep (S. pyogenes) >>> S. aureus

rapidFireQAs.q: More diffuse pink skin lesion + tenderness + fever
rapidFireQAs.a: cellulitis

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of cellulitis
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus exceeds S. pyogenes

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of erysipelas + cellulitis
rapidFireQAs.a: oral dicloxacillin or oral cephalexin

rapidFireQAs.q: Vesicles anywhere on body (not limited for extensors) + Celiac
rapidFireQAs.a: dermatitis herpetiformis

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M goes hiking + linear vesicles on calf appearing days later
rapidFireQAs.a: contact dermatitis = type IV hypersensitivity; linear vesicles = poison ivy/sumac

rapidFireQAs.q: 38F gardens a lot + gets rash on face, arms, backs of hands
rapidFireQAs.a: contact dermatitis from sunscreen

rapidFireQAs.q: Type III HS → Ab-Ag complexes
rapidFireQAs.a: Serum sickness → immune complexes depositing in joints several days after drug or infection Arthus reaction → localized cutaneous type III HS → skin reaction/rash at injection site several days after administration of agent → key point is that it’s not immediate; in type I hypersensitivity, we’d get an immediate reaction; in Arthus reaction, it takes a few days Super HY is postinfectious arthritis → arthritis due to HepB, HepC, rubella, Yersinia enterocolitica, etc. → immune complex deposition in joints → this is considered a serum sickness Erythema nodosum → panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) due to immune complex deposition → USMLE likes Crohn disease, sulfa drugs, Strep infections, and Coccidioidomycosis as causes. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) → can occur after skin infections as well (i.e., impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis)

rapidFireQAs.q: Type IV hypersensitivity → T cell-mediated response (delayed)
rapidFireQAs.a: Contact dermatitis (nickel [wristwatches], sunscreen, poison ivy/sumac, rubber PPD test for TB Multiple sclerosis (T cell attack against oligodendrocytes in white matter) Stevens-Johnson syndrome; toxic epidermal necrolysis

rapidFireQAs.q: Most important prognostic factor for melanoma
rapidFireQAs.a: depth of lesion

rapidFireQAs.q: Recommendation to prevent melanoma
rapidFireQAs.a: avoid sun or use protective clothing (sounds absurdly obvious, but I’ve seen students choose wrong answers like use SPF30)

rapidFireQAs.q: Farmer/fisherman/construction worker + red, scaly lesion on ear/forehead; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: actinic keratosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Above patient with ulcerated lesion emerging from the red scaly lesion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SCC → need to know actinic keratosis is precursor to SCC

rapidFireQAs.q: Risk factor for SCC apart from the sun
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE is obsessed with immunodeficiency and smoking, even for cutaneous SCC

rapidFireQAs.q: Biopsy of SCC?
rapidFireQAs.a: keratin pearls + intercellular bridges

rapidFireQAs.q: Old scar or burn + new ulcerated lesion
rapidFireQAs.a: SCC (Marjolin ulcer) → chronically irritated area / burn / scar can lead to SCC (when I was in MS4 I saw an older woman with a Marjolin ulcer on her chin from a chickenpox scar she had since she was a kid)

rapidFireQAs.q: Ulcerated lesion on nose or pinna of ear + rolled/heaped-up edges
rapidFireQAs.a: BCC

rapidFireQAs.q: Ulcerated lesion + telangiectasia visible
rapidFireQAs.a: BCC

rapidFireQAs.q: Biopsy of BCC?
rapidFireQAs.a: islands and nests of basophilic cells (dark purple)

rapidFireQAs.q: Antibodies in pemphigus vulgaris?
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-desmoglein (anti-desmosome) → desmosomes enable adjacent cell-to-cell adhesion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Antibodies in bullous pemphigoid
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-hemidesmosome → hemidesmosomes secure the dermis to the epidermal basal layer.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which one is worse, bullous pemphigoid or pemphigus vulgaris?
rapidFireQAs.a: pemphigus vulgaris; why? → PV gets bullae on the skin that rupture with friction (Nikolsky sign) + scar → oral mucosal involvement is more prevalent in PV.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most likely organism causing impetigo
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus now exceeds Group A Strep for non-bullous (“regular”) impetigo; for bullous, S. aureus has always exceeded S. pyogenes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Golden crusty lesions around the mouth in school-age child
rapidFireQAs.a: impetigo, not HSV.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + sharply demarcated fiery red lesion extending from the knee to ankle + fever of 101F
rapidFireQAs.a: erysipelas → a Dx students never remember well → not as bad as cellulitis → erysipelas is infection of superficial dermis +/- dermal lymphatics, whereas cellulitis is hypodermis; the superficial nature of erysipelas gives it a well-demarcated, fiery appearance, whereas cellulitis is more diffuse and pink.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common organism for erysipelas?
rapidFireQAs.a: Group A Strep far exceeds S. aureus (but do not neglect the latter).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common organism for cellulitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus exceeds Group A Strep.

rapidFireQAs.q: Treatment for erysipelas + cellulitis
rapidFireQAs.a: oral dicloxacillin or oral cephalexin → both agents cover Staph + Strep; penicillin only covers Strep.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + started taking high-dose vitamins past few months as part of new dietary regimen + has cracked lips, rough/dry skin, and alopecia on scalp; these findings are due to excess of which vitamin?
rapidFireQAs.a: vitamin A → can cause desquamation, increased hepatic transaminases, dyslipidemia, and pseudotumor cerebri (increased intracranial pressure); teratogenic; must do pregnancy test before commencing isotretinoin for acne.

rapidFireQAs.q: 74M + lesion on cheek showing neoplastic cells with dense pigment granules; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: melanoma. Sounds like pigmented BCC, but USMLE wants melanoma for this description. BCC histologically can be described as having islands and nests of basophilic cells; squamous cell carcinoma has keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pic is shown of cavitating lung cancer; what’s the diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: squamous cell carcinoma; can present with cavitary/cavitating lesion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + Hx of heavy smoking/alcohol + new-onset dysphagia; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus; heavy smoking/alcohol are major risk factors; do immediate endoscopy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Family Med Q shows glowing red rash on face in someone being treated for acne; Q asks best way to minimize this condition
rapidFireQAs.a: avoidance of sun exposure; topic tretinoin (vitamin A) can cause photosensitivity (usually red rash); oral tetracycline sometimes used for acne tends to cause more of a blistering photosensitivity. Oral isotretinoin (high-dose vitamin A used for severe acne) is big risk teratogen; must do pregnancy test + recommend contraception before commencing.

rapidFireQAs.q: 60F + high calcium + lung cancer; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: squamous cell carcinoma secreting PTHrp.
